One often encounters the idea that irregular connections should be viewed as “degenerations” of logarithmic connections, as singular points coalesce. Whilst this viewpoint may be useful for some purposes,
it is hard to relate the moduli spaces which appear before and after the coalescence.Rather, the first example of an irregular connection to have in mind should probably be that which arises by taking the Fourier–Laplace transform of a logarithmic connection on the Riemann sphere.
The basic fact that the function {{formula:8a23fd6d-8403-49b9-9ab4-b9b932d7f053}} satisfies the differential equation
{{formula:ba1f98b0-b31e-4257-b205-f70fea38c9cc}}which has a pole of order two at {{formula:9dc89b45-548f-4db2-8567-cc9e832d3d97}} , implies that the Fourier–Laplace transform of a solution of a logarithmic connection will be a solution of an irregular connection (see for a basic class of examples). And moreover by considering stability conditions etc this can be shown to induce an algebraic isomorphism between the corresponding De Rham moduli spaces (and between the corresponding Betti spaces).
In such cases the irregular connections that arise have only two poles on the Riemann sphere, a pole of order one and a pole of order two.
Thus the simplest irregular moduli spaces are in fact isomorphic to the logarithmic case (so the moduli spaces are certainly not more “degenerate” in the irregular case—this is also reflected in the fact that irregular moduli spaces admit complete hyperkähler metrics.) In general of course there will be many moduli spaces (even on the Riemann sphere), that are not isomorphic to a logarithmic case.Another aspect of this example of the Fourier–Laplace transform, that motivated the definition of irregular curve, is the fact that on the logarithmic side the moduli of the curve basically amounts to the positions of the poles (and we know that their motion underlies many of the known braid group actions), whereas on the isomorphic irregular side there are only two poles (so have no moduli), but there is a nontrivial irregular type at the pole of order two: the choice of the pole positions on the logarithmic side matches up precisely with the choice of the irregular type on the irregular side, i.e. the moduli of the (irregular) curves on each side matches up.
(Moreover the isomonodromy equations/braiding etc match up—this may be understood in terms of Harnad's duality which can be shown to be equivalent to Fourier–Laplace (cf. §3, ).

Some other possible approaches to such questions are as follows.
i) Recall that Cosgrove (e.g. in ) has done much work classifying higher order equations with the Painlevé property although his approach seems difficult for higher rank equations (e.g. sixth order).
ii) On the other hand Malgrange and
Umemura have introduced a nonlinear differential Galois theory which one might hope would help with such classification, although it turns out that the strength of their theory is its vast generality and present results suggest it does not even distinguish amongst the six Painlevé equations themselves (when they have generic parameters).One could see this attempt to classify such nonlinear algebraic differential equations as a basic step in “differential algebraic geometry”—the extension of algebraic geometry obtained by allowing derivatives in the equations—the isomonodromy equations should form a basic class of objects to be studied, much as abelian varieties or Calabi–Yau manifolds are in classical algebraic geometry. On the other hand one can view this subject as a half-way step to “noncommutative algebraic geometry”.4) In essence we are associating what might be called a “wild nonabelian Hodge structure” to a certain class of graphs with some extra data on them. This structure consists of a hyperkähler manifold {{formula:8d7dcc79-4101-4ac4-9b77-4eec09b269a4}} (as in ) which in one complex structure is a moduli space of meromorphic connections and in another is a space of meromorphic Higgs bundles. The isomonodromy system is naturally associated to this structure (it controls the isomonodromic deformations of the meromorphic connections). It seems that the work of S. Szabo (interpreting certain Fourier–Laplace transforms as Nahm transforms) can be extended to show that the full hyperkähler metric is also preserved by all the Kac–Moody Weyl group symmetries.

canonical commutation relations. Amongst several possibilities, one of the most promising and

a minimal observable momentum {{formula:0fc8810e-a626-4583-a9d2-bc333d831350}} .Since the UV/IR mixing allows one to probe high-energy physics by low-energy one, it justifies
the use of quantum mechanics in the presence of a minimal length. Investigating the influence
of the minimal length assumption on the energy spectrum of quantum systems has become

minimal length may also be useful to describe non-pointlike particles, such

There is a belief that if quantum gravity effects are

input: What are the differences in how triangular, boxcar, and novel spike-time-based surrogate gradients are utilized in SNN training, and how do their distinct properties impact the training outcomes across various neural network architectures?
expected_output:
The differences in how triangular, boxcar, and novel spike-time-based surrogate gradients are utilized in SNN training lie in their distinct mathematical formulations and the properties they impart to the training process. Triangular surrogate gradients, as described, are defined by the equation \frac{\partial H \left(x \right)}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{\gamma ^2} \max \left(0, \gamma - \left|x-V_\mathrm {th} \right| \right), where \gamma is a constraint factor and V_\mathrm {th} is the threshold of the IF neuron. This formulation allows for a smooth approximation of the gradient around the threshold, facilitating the training of SNNs by mitigating the non-differentiability issue inherent in the Heaviside function used in spiking neurons.

In contrast, the boxcar surrogate gradient function is defined as \frac{\delta s[t]}{\delta u[t]} = 0.5 if |u[t] - \theta | \le 0.5 and 0 otherwise, providing a simpler, step-like approximation of the gradient. This simplicity can make the training process more straightforward but might not capture the nuances of neural behavior as effectively as the triangular formulation.

The novel spike-time-based surrogate gradient technique, on the other hand, utilizes the spike time information in the derivative, offering a more nuanced approach to approximating gradients. This method computes the gradient at each timestep based on the output spike, membrane potential, and the time difference since the last spike, incorporating more dynamic information about the neural activity. This could potentially lead to more accurate training outcomes, especially in networks where the timing of spikes carries significant information.

The distinct properties of these surrogate gradients impact the training outcomes across various neural network architectures in several ways. Firstly, the choice of surrogate gradient can affect the convergence speed and stability of the training process. For instance, the triangular and novel spike-time-based gradients might offer smoother and more stable training dynamics compared to the boxcar function, due to their more gradual and informed approximation of the gradients.

Secondly, the ability to capture and utilize the temporal aspects of spiking activity can significantly influence the performance of SNNs, especially in tasks that require precise timing or rate coding. The novel spike-time-based surrogate gradient, by incorporating spike timing information, might be particularly advantageous in such scenarios, potentially leading to better accuracy and more efficient training.

Lastly, the compatibility of these surrogate gradients with different neural network architectures, such as those incorporating both IF and LIF neurons, can also impact the training outcomes. The hybrid training procedure that combines surrogate-gradient training with ANN-SNN conversion might offer a versatile approach, allowing for the initialization of weights and thresholds in complex networks and reducing the number of timesteps required for training without compromising accuracy.

In summary, the differences in triangular, boxcar, and novel spike-time-based surrogate gradients used in SNN training are rooted in their mathematical formulations and the information they capture about neural activity. These differences can significantly impact the training process, influencing convergence, stability, and ultimately, the performance of the trained network across various architectures and tasks.
context: The overall training algorithm is outlined in Algorithm REF . To address the non-differentiability inherent in training SNNs via back-propagation, we employ the surrogate gradient technique. We choose triangular-shaped surrogate gradients , it can be described as:\frac{\partial H \left(x \right)}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{\gamma ^2} \max \left(0, \gamma - \left|x-V_\mathrm {th} \right| \right),where \gamma is the constraint factor determining the sample range for activating the gradient, while V_\mathrm {th} denotes the threshold of IF neuron. We set \gamma to 1 and V_\mathrm {th} to 1.The final loss function is expressed as:\mathcal {L}_\mathrm {all} = \mathcal {L}_\mathrm {CE} + \lambda \mathcal {L}_\mathrm {SKD},where \mathcal {L}_\mathrm {CE} denotes cross-entropy loss, while \lambda signifies a hyper-parameter to adjust the proportion of \mathcal {L}_\mathrm {SKD}.

In order to take advantage of the standard backpropagation-based optimization procedures, authors in, introduced the surrogate gradient technique. The input-output characteristics of an LIF (or IF) neuron is a step function, the gradient of which is discontinuous at the threshold point (Fig. REF ). In surrogate gradient technique, the gradient is approximated by pseudo-derivatives like linear or exponential functions. Authors in proposed a novel approximation function for these gradients by utilizing the spike time information in the derivative. The gradient at timestep {{formula:10d55c09-a59b-470e-87ec-f11eabdb7c39}} is computed as follows:
{{formula:ced6cb56-c3f8-41e1-9b23-726012ab2adc}}Here, {{formula:ed5c232f-198b-4e2d-b974-e1fc99bdafd6}} is the output spike at time {{formula:7e5cbc7d-edfb-4a2c-be87-62c7b45a57fc}} , {{formula:ddaa3c79-eba9-43cc-9097-7fb012787c66}} is the membrane potential at {{formula:3d384b3f-b9e2-481b-953e-06893d2275c9}} , {{formula:037235db-e16f-4ce8-ba69-a8a607d083c9}} is the difference between current timestep and the last timestep post-neuron generated a spike. {{formula:307360e7-8764-4494-965e-cf1aa787c6b3}} and {{formula:395d0fc3-39d5-42a7-b1b8-76ace04023aa}} are hyperparameters. Once the neuron gradients are approximated, backpropagation through time (BPTT) is performed using the chain rule of derivatives. In BPTT, the network is unrolled over all timesteps. The final output is computed as the cumulation of outputs at every timestep and eventually, loss is defined on the summed output. During backward propagation of the loss, the gradients are accumulated over time and used in gradient-descent optimization. Authors in proposed a hybrid training procedure in which the surrogate-gradient training is preceded by an ANN-SNN conversion to initialize the weights and thresholds of the network. The advantage of this method over ANN-SNN conversion is twofold: one can train a network with both IF and LIF neurons and the number of timesteps required for training is reduced by a factor of 10 without losing accuracy.

input: How do Betti curves of random symmetric matrices compare to geometric ones in terms of their topological features and computational complexities?
expected_output: Betti curves of random symmetric matrices and geometric ones exhibit distinct topological features due to the differences in their underlying structures. Random symmetric matrices have Betti curves that are consistent and similar in organization, indicating that most matrix orderings have a similar arrangement of cliques. In contrast, geometric matrices, which are obtained as the distance matrix of sample points randomly distributed on a manifold, have Betti curves that are dramatically different due to the non-uniform sampling of possible matrix orderings. The computational complexity of calculating Betti curves for random symmetric matrices is generally lower than for geometric matrices, as the former can be generated and analyzed more straightforwardly. However, the topological features of geometric matrices, such as those derived from Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic spaces, can provide valuable insights into the underlying geometric properties of the data, making their computation worthwhile despite the increased complexity. Overall, the comparison of Betti curves between random and geometric symmetric matrices highlights the importance of considering the underlying structure and distribution of the data when analyzing topological features and computational complexities.
context:
Any matrix ordering {{formula:70160249-c94e-4216-a4d0-9f7b25e39c96}} appears with equal probability in the distribution of random symmetric matrices with i.i.d. entries. The consistency of the Betti curves in Figure 6a indicates that “most” of these matrix orderings have a similar organization of cliques. For geometric matrices, the possible matrix orderings are sampled in a highly non-uniform manner, leading to dramatically different Betti curves.
Despite this, it is worth noting that any matrix ordering can in fact arise from a distance matrix.Definition 4.1 A set of points {{formula:473305ca-df86-482b-9b4e-efdf719b527f}} is called a geometric realization of the matrix ordering {{formula:d3e487b9-2f46-4050-9fa9-bd92f76928b6}} if the distance matrix {{formula:0f0bbc49-6ea9-4e7d-9fe7-f7ae80ac1196}} has {{formula:f4f37ac3-7e00-4b29-9cf2-b5edc0820099}} .Note that for each collection of three or more points, the (higher) triangle inequalities implied by the metric impose strong constraints on {{formula:a2ee0776-c2f3-442a-bea2-fd7fe6203e77}} .
This means that for most matrix orderings, the probability of sampling a point configuration in the unit cube that yields a geometric realization of {{formula:bc7d257f-c328-408a-ac07-bab4b46f856c}} is vanishingly small. This is why geometric Betti curves are, on average, so different from those of random matrices. Nevertheless, geometric realizations do always exist, provided {{formula:21aaf182-8d7e-4ccd-9c42-dd6ac9d310d6}} .Lemma 4.2 Every {{formula:5d8ad796-76d9-4304-9ab5-c87e283cf1db}} matrix ordering {{formula:2ae71549-2047-40af-8569-9fe6304e8efe}} that has {{formula:77267456-df95-4fc1-82b7-310ec898f4f9}} distinct off-diagonal entries possesses a geometric realization in {{formula:2bc34fc0-2855-4278-a8b3-966ce2a3d839}} -dimensional Euclidean space.

We call random any symmetric matrix with identically independent real-valued entries, geometric any symmetric matrix which is obtained as the distance matrix of sample points randomly distributed on a manifold, and correlation matrix any symmetric matrix obtained as the (Pearson) correlation matrix of given time series. When dealing with geometric and correlation matrices, we shall consider
the case of points sampled from the fundamental metric spaces \mathbb {R}^n (Euclidean space), \mathbb {S}^n (a sphere), and \mathbb {H}^n (a hyperbolic space). It is known that these are the geometric models of the simply connected n-manifolds of constant scalar curvature 0, 1 and -1, respectively.
[Figure: Standard geodesic triangles in Euclidean, spherical and hyperbolic space.]Generally speaking, the geometric properties of a manifold, endowed with different underlying metrics, can be very different. First and foremost, geodesic triangles in the three fundamental models, have different behaviours: if triangles in the Euclidean space are “straight”, they get “fatter” on a sphere and “thinner” in a hyperbolic space – cf. Figure REF . An analytical description of the metrics in these geometries is given in the Supplementary. In practical examples, and in our results, we consider sample points randomly distributed in the unit cube, on the unit sphere or in
the hyperbolic space and then compute the Betti curves described in Section REF .We call random any symmetric matrix with identically independent real-valued entries, geometric any symmetric matrix which is obtained as the distance matrix of sample points uniformly, randomly, distributed on a manifold, and correlation matrix any symmetric matrix obtained as the (Pearson) correlation matrix of given time series.The Betti curves can reliably detect both the Euclidean geometry and the random structure of symmetric matrices – see ; in our work we complement this observation by exploring the case of spherical and hyperbolic geometries, together with the case of correlation matrices. We review here their definitions.

We also consider a related approximate realisation problem, with different information. As for a random geometric graph, we start with a family of {{formula:5579a9d1-994d-4da2-94f5-4ff14f788ec0}} unseen points {{formula:3d3bf4ef-d977-4404-be3b-c36e26a6c049}} independently and uniformly distributed in the square {{formula:aac3440f-5195-4b8e-b233-d4d9d1461679}} , forming the hidden embedding {{formula:fdc2893b-8c10-4e90-941d-d722a70899cd}} . (There is no radius {{formula:999247c2-810e-4dc5-ac43-bada34f306b8}} here, and there is no graph.)
We are given, for each vertex {{formula:603363c1-66bf-4bfb-9d49-0e65c2d761cf}} , the ordering {{formula:8921a93a-3a1b-45e9-9904-b1f7e7a862b5}} 
of the vertices by increasing Euclidean distance from {{formula:13c0daa3-2f72-42e5-8360-5ecba44e50fd}} . This is the family of vertex orderings corresponding to {{formula:4b1a897c-5970-4b94-bb5c-a3a10c5fc7d1}} .
Notice that with probability 1 no two distances between distinct points will be equal.
Notice also that, if we had access to the complete ordering of the Euclidean distances between all pairs of distinct vertices in the hidden embedding {{formula:d34cfab8-f446-4322-8e6b-501523b10022}} , then we could read off the family of vertex orderings.We shall see that, by using the family of vertex orderings, we can with high probability find an embedding with displacement error dramatically better than the bound we obtain for random geometric graphs.

input: What is the best way to ensure compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks, such as EU GDPR, US HIPAA, and US FISMA, in a unified approach to data protection?
expected_output: To ensure compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks, such as EU GDPR, US HIPAA, and US FISMA, in a unified approach to data protection, it is essential to establish a comprehensive framework that addresses the requirements of each regulation. This can be achieved by setting guidelines and regulations that define transparent and fair data collection, as seen in the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe and the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act in the US. Additionally, implementing a hierarchical cybersecurity model, such as the one suggested by Strielkina et al. for healthcare IoT systems, can help encompass relationships between different regulations and provide tool support for corresponding decision-making. Furthermore, using multiple regulations to extract penalty clauses and train machine learning models for automated identification and deconstruction of penalty clauses, as done by Anish et al., can also be an effective approach. Ultimately, a unified approach to data protection requires a thorough understanding of the regulatory landscape and the implementation of best practices and standards that cater to the specific needs of healthcare organizations and public administrations.
context: 260 out of 280 studies have mentioned at least one regulation in the context of their research. We summarize the regulations considered in the studies in Table REF together with additional information important for the discussion. In some cases primary studies described a wide range of different regulations from the same regulator, such as US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standards (mentioned in 11 studies) and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations (mentioned in seven studies). Some of the regulations mentioned in less than five primary studies were as follows Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act (US CDPA), Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (US COPPA), EU Cybersecurity Act, the EU In Vitro Diagnostics Regulation (EU IVDR), US Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act (US HITECH) , US executive order 13960 , US executive order 14028 , EU Markets in Financial Instruments Directive 2014/65/EU (EU MiFID II) , US Sarbanes–Oxley Act (US SOX) . Some other rarely considered regulations were Chinese Cybersecurity Law , US Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) , US Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002 (US FISMA) . While the majority of the studies mentioned the demand to be compliant with two or more regulations simultaneously, only some explicitly addressed this demand with corresponding PPs. For example, Joshi et al.  have considered multiple regulations (such as EU GDPR, US HIPAA, US FISMA, ISO 27001, ISO 27002 along with other non-regulatory types of sources of requirements like OAUTH, COBIT), but only within the RE process area. Strielkina et al. suggested a hierarchical cybersecurity model for healthcare IoT systems encompassing relationships between different regulations and tool support for the corresponding decision-making. Anish et al. used multiple regulations to extract penalty clauses and train their ML model for automated identification and deconstruction of penalty clauses.

We explored the information available on the main official sources of European, International, and National regulators (e.g., ENISA, NIST, Salute.gov)
using main searched keywords such as cybersecurity, privacy, electronic health record (EHR), medical device, telemedicine, cloud for healthcare.A second round of research was conducted using the main indexing platforms (e.g., Elsevier Scopus, Google scholar, IEEE Xplore), and the primary searched keywords were: cybersecurity in healthcare, healthcare cybersecurity legislation, telemedicine security and privacy, cybersecurity of medical devices; security framework for healthcare. We performed a forward and backward analysis for each document or paper collected.
Afterward, to refine the research, we constrained each collected document to two key requirements:
(i) the regulation must be in effect, (ii) the document must address data security, privacy issues, or cybersecurity measures for healthcare organizations or public administrations.
Therefore, we did not include works that address only manufacturers of medical devices, external service providers, or government agencies.Examples of documents excluded, as not deemed of interest, are ISO/TR 17522:2015 Health informatics — Provisions for health applications on mobile/smart devices , focused only on interoperability, and ISO 14971:2019 Medical devices — Application of risk management to medical devices  that is specifically addressed to manufacturers of medical devices.Results.
This step allowed us to gather 68 potential documents of interest first, then narrowed to 49 documents by considering the key requirements.
The final corpus, therefore, is composed of 11 regulations, 21 best practices, and 17 standards gathered by European (9), international (19), and national (21) sources.

We provide the following recommendations for regulators and policy makers:Set guidelines and regulations that define transparent and fair data collection. For example, in Europe there is the General Data Protection Regulation , and in the US, there is the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) . The latter sets certain requirements for online services directed to children. With the rapid uptake of digital technologies and lack of data collection regulations, non-regulated data collection by third parties can be harmful in the long run. It may normalise sharing personal data with third parties. Having said that, regulations such as GDPR and COPPA have their own technical and non-technical issues, such as the challenges in monitoring compliance, which may need non-conventional tools. For example, Reyes et al.  found many apps available in the US are violating COPPA. Nevertheless, we can learn from them and work towards improving their issues.

input: What are the advantages of using CNNs over FCNNs in feature extraction tasks, and how do these advantages impact their performance in practice?
expected_output:
The advantages of using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) over Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNNs) in feature extraction tasks are primarily due to their ability to respect translation symmetry and extract local features explicitly. CNNs achieve this through the use of convolutional layers, which apply filters to small regions of the input data, allowing them to capture local patterns and features. This is particularly beneficial in tasks where the data has spatial or temporal hierarchies, such as image or signal processing. In contrast, FCNNs treat all input data equally, without considering spatial or temporal relationships, which can lead to poor performance in tasks that require the extraction of local features.

The advantages of CNNs over FCNNs impact their performance in practice in several ways. Firstly, CNNs are able to achieve higher accuracy in feature extraction tasks, as they are able to capture local patterns and features more effectively. This is evident in the context, where the CNN outperforms the FCNN in predicting winding numbers, even in cases where the winding numbers are larger than those seen during training. Secondly, CNNs are able to generalize better to new, unseen data, as they are able to extract features that are invariant to translation and other transformations. This is demonstrated in the context, where the CNN is able to predict winding numbers accurately, even in cases where the input data is different from that seen during training.

Furthermore, the use of convolutional layers in CNNs allows for the extraction of features at multiple scales, which can be beneficial in tasks where the data has multiple spatial or temporal hierarchies. This is evident in the context, where the CNN is able to extract features from the input data at multiple scales, allowing it to predict winding numbers accurately. In contrast, FCNNs are limited in their ability to extract features at multiple scales, as they treat all input data equally.

Overall, the advantages of CNNs over FCNNs in feature extraction tasks make them a more effective choice for a wide range of applications, including image and signal processing, natural language processing, and more. Their ability to respect translation symmetry, extract local features explicitly, and generalize well to new data make them a powerful tool for extracting relevant features from complex data.
context:
The test results of two neural networks are presented in Table. REF , which shows a very high accuracy (more than {{formula:0fe735f8-4f30-4d29-bc73-9073f14a0a21}} ) of the CNN and FCNN on the test data set with the winding numbers {{formula:8dd7790f-3810-48d0-8909-c8af8c1ea871}} . We can find that the CNN performs generally better than the FCNN. Surprisingly, the CNN works well even in the cases of {{formula:e7e60315-fc11-44c2-9824-1b386664e1e0}} , which consist of configurations with larger winding numbers not seen by neural networks during the training. On the contrary, the FCNN cannot predict the true winding numbers even though it has more trainable parameters. These results indicate that the convolutional layer respects the translation symmetry of complex spectrum in the momentum space explicitly and convolutional layers can take local winding angle {{formula:46e4aa2b-edb5-4454-93a2-ea9a51399f6c}} explicitly through the {{formula:b65535be-b930-4239-baa9-8510f4a18e62}} kernels.To further see the advantage of the CNN, we open up the black box of neural networks and find the relationship between intermediate activation values and physical quantities, i.e. the winding angle {{formula:8aa93106-e29b-4393-9582-9357ea2d065d}} . Based on the convolutional layers, we consider that the activation value after two convolutions should have a linear dependence on {{formula:812e9b8a-c4fe-4ff6-b46b-46ea830cd10e}} to some extent and the following fully-connected layers use a simple linear regression. We plot {{formula:27f358b4-0f2f-4588-938e-50350f4e7571}} versus {{formula:244434c9-5b64-4ef0-9d87-56726b07570f}} , with {{formula:aba78006-b52f-47e5-a41f-53c57163b54e}} and {{formula:475a43d4-be74-472d-9056-55fd77e70dc1}} being the {{formula:7fa6b793-e723-4994-bafa-70dc0a923a8b}} -th component of intermediate values after two convolution layers. As shown in Fig. REF (c), the intermediate output is approximately linear with {{formula:07ef8317-cae3-4a77-8ab4-5bc1e7867070}} within certain regions. A linear combination of these intermediate values with correct coefficients in the following fully connected layers can then easily lead to the true winding number. In this way, the CNN realizes a calculation workflow that is equivalent to the wingding angle {{formula:9e059bd3-7a4d-485d-b8c5-5c4ce073c0cc}} in Eq. (REF ).
[Table: Accuracy of the CNN and FCNN on test data set with the winding numbers w={±1,±2,±3,±4,±5}w= \lbrace \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4, \pm 5\rbrace in the Hatano-Nelson model with μ=1,2,3,4,5\mu =1,2,3,4,5.

Figure REF shows an example of the training and validation Loss curves of one of our CNNs.
[Figure: (color online). Training and validation Loss curves of a CNN algorithm of this work. The model converged approximately after 18 epochs and both training and validation performance remained equivalent. This suggests that the CNN has learned how to solve the problem.]As can be noticed, in this case the network training reached the best performance at around 18 epochs, where the Loss is well reduced and becomes almost flat. The validation exhibit a similar trend and confirms the success of the CNN training. It is important to mention that the training process needs to be done only once. The trained model can be used for the analysis of a full experiment, or even for other experiments with the same electronic settings.The algorithm developed in this work is divided in three main steps: baseline correction, deconvolution, peak detection and integration. The architecture of the CNNs is presented in Figure REF . The CNNs have a similar structure to the ones used for image classification. However, in the present case the input data is a one dimensional array of size 512 that corresponds to the number of time buckets of a digital signal. The output of the baseline and deconvolution CNNs is a signal of the same size as the input data (see Figure REF ). Nevertheless, the output of the third CNN is a classification score map, with values between 0 and 1 at each time bucket (the closer to 1 the more likely the bucket corresponds to a peak).Typical CNNs consist of a number of convolutional layers, eventually intercalated with Max Pooling layers, and followed at the end by a number of fully connected layers. A convolutional layer consists of {{formula:28342fcc-b996-4d89-8a4b-7408b9e8d51a}} filter masks and it computes the convolution operation between the input array and each filter mask (also called kernel). The output of a convolutional layer is, therefore, a set of {{formula:fdd298ce-4239-4c8e-81a6-4c8649d9ffca}} filtered signals. The resulting filtering effect depends on the mask size and values; a filter may enhance some features of the input signal. Thus, the output of convolutional layers is commonly known as feature maps. For instance, in the baseline correction network, the input is of dimension {{formula:1c7a1a69-e11c-4029-8930-24c52994ef45}} meaning one signal with 512 buckets, while the output of the first convolutional layer is of dimension {{formula:9ee60e77-dca8-49c5-ba90-8165e72822e0}} , meaning 32 signals with 512 buckets (or a signal of size 512 with 32 channels). The number of filters, {{formula:cf55f450-4a20-4a57-94ef-2a322f7d7382}} , is an empirical value that is chosen to improve the performance of the CNN.The size of the kernels were chosen between 17 and 21 buckets to fully cover a peak region. Note that due to the finite size of the signals, the convolution operation can not be applied to the points in its extremities (first and last time buckets). In convolutional layers, if the output signal size must be equal to the input signal size, then padding (artificially adding sufficient number of points in both extremities, usually filled with zeros) is employed.

The primary advantage of the proposed neural network is the feature extraction capability of the convolutional neural network (CNN) (Fig. REF ). The CNN is able to distill information from the boundary layer profiles in a physically consistent manner, i.e., by considering the boundary layer profiles as continuous functions and by encoding the information into a set of parameters indicated by the (green) shaded neurons {{formula:60dcd64c-b2f3-4047-8806-9c37de9c31b4}} in Fig. REF b. The CNN provides a mapping from the space of boundary layer profiles to the physical parameter space in an automated, data-driven fashion, i.e., without requiring the user to specify an explicitly defined learning target for the CNN. To demonstrate this capability of the proposed neural network, we consider the case where the CNN maps the distilled information from the boundary layer profile {{formula:3a80075f-9390-4298-b592-b4598ff169cc}} to a single parameter {{formula:9d2fb4f2-d0c6-4caa-8836-766e4e2bceaf}} at the interface between the CNN and the fully connected network in Fig.  REF . In essence, this process mimics the behavior of the fully-connected network A from Table II by choosing the CNN parameters to encode a single feature from the boundary layer profiles. Because the CNN does not make any prior assumptions about what this single feature should be, one might expect that the predictive performance of the CNN architecture {{formula:3f34025a-19f0-4f33-8d46-cbcd7b4952fb}} would be better than that of the fully connected network {{formula:c9c5f75b-be68-48cb-aed9-15d379b1e4bd}} . Somewhat surprisingly, however, comparison of the respective testing errors for the asymmetrical NLF-0416 airfoil indicates that the network {{formula:0b41e9a0-200f-447e-a388-32e638c664dd}} performs slightly better than {{formula:6db99837-126b-4e22-b9f7-405b362e07a5}} (testing error of 21.2% versus 24.5%). The explanation of this relative performance is left as a topic for future studies. However, it does seem to provide independent evidence that supports the practice of using the analytically defined shape factor {{formula:bf480374-40e5-49d8-aa31-e597377c5508}} as a nearly optimal scalar representation of the boundary layer profile for the purpose of predicting the amplification rates. Next, we evaluated the parameter {{formula:de63d39a-a0f7-4067-8128-d67674eb743a}} for each of the 111 boundary layer profiles along the upper surface of the asymmetrical NLF-0416 airfoil by using the convolutional neural network model that was trained on the full Falkner-Skan database. For convenience of interpretation, we normalize (i.e., shift and scale) the learned parameter {{formula:e4abbb38-1aef-4381-83a5-7d4c66b84f45}} to {{formula:bc1a1634-c2ab-48bb-96ce-7850accc2b70}} such that the latter falls within the range of [0, 1].

input: What metrics are commonly used across different studies to assess the goodness-of-fit of topic models, and how do they compare in evaluating model performance?
expected_output: The commonly used evaluation metrics to assess the goodness-of-fit of topic models include statistical measures that evaluate how well the model captures the underlying structure of the data. These metrics are applicable to all topic models and are used to evaluate the model's performance in terms of its ability to model the data accurately. The two main approaches to evaluating a topic model are evaluating its performance on a specific task, such as making predictions, and statistically evaluating the model's goodness-of-fit. The proposed model has been shown to improve the accuracy of topic prediction by up to 12.99% compared to existing feature extraction and topic modeling approaches. However, the specific metrics used to evaluate the goodness-of-fit of topic models are not explicitly stated in the provided context, but it is mentioned that the section will present some commonly used evaluation metrics applicable to all topic models.
context: In this section we investigate in how far the fitted topic model captures our concepts of policy topics, with special attention to the tax (increase and decrease) topics. We first evaluate the two steps of constructing tax topics in detail. Next, we also briefly consider the other topics in order to understand how well the topic model captures the general essence of the speeches.

input: Does long-wave IR truly outperform near-IR in low-light object detection across various environmental conditions, and can its advantages be consistently observed in different experimental setups?
expected_output: The long-wave infrared camera is more suitable for recognition, security, and vehicle driving scenes because the radiation band of the human body is within its range. This suggests that long-wave IR has inherent advantages over near-IR in certain applications, particularly those involving human detection and low-light conditions. However, the provided context does not directly compare the performance of long-wave IR and near-IR in low-light object detection across various environmental conditions. It does mention that the IRVI dataset, which uses long-wave IR equipment, is designed for unpaired video translation between nighttime infrared videos and daytime visible ones, implying its potential usefulness in low-light scenarios. Additionally, datasets like FLIR and KAIST, which involve infrared and visible light data, are used for object detection tasks, but the context does not explicitly state that long-wave IR outperforms near-IR in these tasks. Therefore, while long-wave IR may have theoretical advantages, the context does not provide conclusive evidence of its consistent outperformance of near-IR in low-light object detection across different experimental setups.

Besides, both FLIR and KAIST (DAY ROAD) are used to evaluate the ability of the model on object detection. On the contrary, our InfraredCity and InfraredCity-Lite are collected for the unpaired video translation between nighttime infrared videos and daytime visible ones.

In general, infrared sensors include two types: near-infrared camera and long-wave infrared camera. The radiation band of the human body is within the range of the latter one. Therefore, the long-wave infrared camera is more in line with the requirements of recognition, security, and vehicle driving scenes. We use the long-wave type equipments to collect data.[Table: The structure of IRVI][Table: Datasets Comparision Information]The dataset collects video streams through a binocular infrared color camera (DTC equipment) and performs scene alignment on the two domains at the hardware level. In different periods, the infrared and visible light data of traffic and monitoring scenes are obtained through vehicle-mounted and fixed-point brackets ways. The detailed comparison information is shown in Table  REF .Specifically, VOT2019-RGBTIR provides 60 video clips, while the duration and quality are varied. Although FLIR offers other infrared and visible light image pairs besides the 4224 frames listed in Table  REF , they are inconsecutive and not counted in as videos. On the other hand, the other three datasets collect for object tracking and detection. Our dataset IRVI is collected for I2V video translation, which contains limited luminance scenes. Moreover, IRVI incorporates monitoring scenes besides traffic, which makes it practical for real-world applications.

KAIST Dataset. KAIST  is a public aligned multispectral pedestrian detection dataset. Due to the problematic annotations in the original dataset, our framework is trained on 8963 image pairs with new annotations and evaluated on 2252 image pairs with the improved annotations . Since the images are misaligned in the original dataset, we use the FLIR-aligned dataset  in our experiment. It has 5142 aligned RGB-IR image pairs, of which 4129 are used for training and 1013 for testing.LLVIP Dataset. LLVIP  is a strictly aligned visible and infrared object detection dataset for low-light vision. It is collected in low-light environments most of which were captured in very dark scenes. It contains 15488 aligned RGB-IR image pairs, of which 12025 images are used for training and 3463 images for testing.

input: What causes feature compression to preserve discriminability and enhance vision task accuracy in certain scenarios?
expected_output: The preservation of discriminability in feature compression is caused by the introduction of a discrimination metric that reduces the feature distance between paired compression and original images in the feature space, thereby mapping the compressed image and the original image to a common feature space with anti-compression characteristics. This is achieved through the use of an adversarial-learning strategy and a metric loss function that encourages the network to extract compression-insensitive features. Additionally, the use of a two-branch network and a metric-learning strategy helps to reduce the feature distance and preserve the discriminability of original features during compression, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of machine vision tasks.
context:
In this paper, we analyzed the feature discriminability in machine vision tasks and addressed its importance in feature compression. Building on this understanding, we introduced a discrimination metric to preserve the discriminability of original features during compression. Through a comparison with the similarity metric, we verified the effectiveness of our proposed discrimination metric. Furthermore, we investigated the trade-off between the discriminability of original features and the proposed discrimination metric.
For future work, we plan to extend the discrimination metric to more machine vision tasks and explore other inter-feature relationships for more feature compression techniques.

In machine learning and computer vision, input images are often filtered to
increase data discriminability. In some situations, however, one may wish to
purposely decrease discriminability of one classification task (a "distractor"
task), while simultaneously preserving information relevant to another (the
task-of-interest): For example, it may be important to mask the identity of
persons contained in face images before submitting them to a crowdsourcing site
(e.g., Mechanical Turk) when labeling them for certain facial attributes.
Another example is inter-dataset generalization: when training on a dataset
with a particular covariance structure among multiple attributes, it may be
useful to suppress one attribute while preserving another so that a trained
classifier does not learn spurious correlations between attributes. In this
paper we present an algorithm that finds optimal filters to give high
discriminability to one task while simultaneously giving low discriminability
to a distractor task. We present results showing the effectiveness of the
proposed technique on both simulated data and natural face images.

expected_output: The Transmission Spectroscopy Metric (TSM) is a method used to compare planets' potential for atmospheric characterization via transmission spectroscopy, and it is proportional to the transmission spectroscopy signal-to-noise. The TSM is based on the strength of a planet's expected spectral features, which are derived from its radius and scale height, as well as the radius of the host star and the host star's apparent J-band magnitude. A higher TSM value indicates a more favorable target for atmospheric characterization. The interplay between TSM, radius, and host star's J magnitude is such that smaller planets with larger host stars and brighter J-band magnitudes tend to have higher TSM values, making them more suitable for transmission spectroscopy. For example, TOI-1231 b has a high TSM value of 99, which ranks it among the highest TSM Neptunes of any temperature, due to its small radius and the bright J-band magnitude of its host star. This suggests that TOI-1231 b is a promising target for atmospheric characterization, and its properties make it an interesting object for further study. Overall, the collective influence of TSM, radius, and host star's J magnitude provides a comprehensive assessment of a celestial object's suitability for atmospheric characterization and helps researchers identify the most promising targets for further investigation.

expected_output: The concept of E_2^{p,q} is a spectral sequence used to construct ℙ¹ extensions in algebraic geometry. Compared to other approaches, such as the Yoneda lemma and Nakayama's lemma, E_2^{p,q} provides a more detailed and explicit way of computing the cohomology groups of the extension. The key similarity between E_2^{p,q} and other approaches is that they all aim to describe the properties of the extension and its relationship to the underlying geometric objects. However, the main difference lies in the level of abstraction and the specific techniques employed. For instance, the Yoneda lemma provides a more general and abstract framework for computing extensions, while E_2^{p,q} is a more concrete and computational tool. In terms of applications, E_2^{p,q} is particularly useful for studying the properties of rational curves and their deformations, whereas other approaches may be more suited for other types of geometric objects or problems. Overall, the choice of approach depends on the specific context and the goals of the investigation.

input: What is the best way to examine the dependence of star formation rates on environment and mass, and how can this be achieved through a synthesis of existing research?
expected_output: To examine the dependence of star formation rates on environment and mass, the best approach is to analyze a large sample of galaxies across various environments, such as clusters and groups, and over a range of redshifts. This can be achieved through a synthesis of existing research by combining data from multiple studies and utilizing techniques such as spectral energy distribution fitting to compute stellar masses, star formation rates, and specific star formation rates. By splitting the sample into different redshift bins and comparing the properties of star-forming and quiescent galaxies at fixed environment and fixed stellar mass, researchers can separate the effects of environment and stellar mass on galaxies. Additionally, examining the correlation between star formation rates and stellar masses, as well as the dependence of star formation rates on projected distance, can provide valuable insights into the role of environment and mass in driving star formation. By synthesizing existing research and utilizing a comprehensive dataset, researchers can construct a detailed star formation history of the universe as a function of galaxy environment, ultimately shedding light on the complex interplay between environment, mass, and star formation rates.

sample in two redshift bins: galaxies at $0.4 < z < 0.6$ and $0.6 < z < 0.9$.
We separate the effects of environment and stellar mass on galaxies by
comparing the properties of star-forming and quiescent galaxies at fixed
environment (projected radius) and fixed stellar mass. For the selected
spectroscopic sample of more than 500 galaxies, the well-known correlation
between SFR and $M_{\rm star}$ is already in place at $z \sim 0.9$, for both SF
and quenched galaxies. Our results are consistent with no evidence that SFR (or
sSFR) depends on environment, suggesting that for cluster galaxies at an
intermediate-to-high redshift range, mass is the primary characteristic that
drives SFR.

Our goal is to construct the star formation history of the universe as a function of galaxy
environment.
Figure REF shows how the mean EW([O2]) within the virial radius depends on environment
and redshift, for our present sample of groups and clusters. Surprisingly, the amount of
emission in clusters is approximately constant with redshift, so the difference between the cluster and
field SFR increases with redshift. This suggests that, at least at cluster densities,
the average SFR is determined by local environment, and not an internal galaxy clock. On the other hand,
galaxy groups at {{formula:8a252b79-47d1-4d6a-8603-1622973f3756}} have SFRs only slightly lower than the expected global average at that redshift.
If SFR is entirely environment-dependent, this means that
the local analogues of these groups should have substantially higher SFRs than the average.

input: What is the comparative sensitivity gain of squeezed light in Sagnac interferometers across different experimental configurations, and how does it impact the overall performance in terms of noise reduction and precision?
expected_output: The comparative sensitivity gain of squeezed light in Sagnac interferometers has been experimentally demonstrated to achieve a nonclassical sensitivity improvement of up to 10 dB, limited by optical loss inside the interferometer. In comparison, measurements performed directly on the squeezed-light laser output revealed squeezing of 10 dB. The Sagnac topology has been shown to surpass the standard quantum limit for a broad spectrum of signal frequencies without the need for filter cavities, making it a powerful option for future gravitational-wave detectors. The use of squeezed light in Sagnac interferometers has the potential to reduce quantum measurement noise and quantum back-action noise, allowing for a considerable increase in displacement sensitivity. This is particularly significant for future detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope, which aim to establish gravitational wave astronomy and require a substantial increase in sensitivity. Overall, the incorporation of squeezed light in Sagnac interferometers offers a promising approach to enhance the performance of gravitational-wave detectors in terms of noise reduction and precision.

The world-wide network of interferometric gravitational wave (GW) detectors is
currently in an
upgrade phase towards what is commonly referred to as the second
generation of detectors. This detector
network is formed of the Advanced LIGO detectors (USA)
, the Advanced Virgo detector (Italy/France) , the
GEO-HF detector (Germany/UK) and the new Japanese KAGRA
observatory . All of these detectors are based on
the classical Michelson topology and
will be limited in their sensitivities by quantum noise over a large range of
frequencies. Quantum noise originates from the quantum
fluctuations of the laser light, which is used for the measurement of GW
induced strain, and manifests as quantum radiation pressure noise (QRPN) and
shot noise, dominating at low and high frequencies, respectively.Michelson-based laser interferometers, cf. figure
REF ,
are so called position meters, i.e. the measured observable is the
position of the test mass mirrors which does not commute with itself at
subsequent moments of time. This non vanishing commutator yields an uncertainty
relation for subsequent position measurements which
enforces the so-called Standard Quantum Limit (SQL).
The notion of the SQL was originally coined by Braginsky and
was believed to set a limit to the achievable sensitivity of a precision
measurement apparatus.
It was later
realised by Braginsky
that it is in fact possible to overcome the SQL by performing a so-called
Quantum Non-Demolition (QND) measurement
, e.g. by introducing cross-correlations in the quantum
noise in an interferometer.
[Figure: Comparison of Michelson with Sagnac interferometer topologies,with arm cavities in both cases. In the Michelson topology the positionsof the mirrors in the two arms of theinterferometer are sensed either by the beam transmitted or the beam reflectedat the beam splitter. However, in the Sagnac interferometer bothbeams, travelling in the clockwise and the counter clockwise direction, sensethe relative positions of all mirrors, though at different times. Consequently,the resulting signal extracted from the main photo detector in the Sagnacinterferometer carries information about the relative velocity of the test massmirrors.]To achieve sensitivities an order
of magnitude higher than in the second generation GW observatories
 requires quantum noise to be reduced. In particular, the
characteristic {{formula:8e49444a-14ba-425c-bb64-b4f0fce09493}} frequency dependence of QRPN causes it to
occlude the low-frequency band which contains a rich population of potential
sources .
An important cornerstone in the designs of GW detectors beyond the second
generation, such as the planned Einstein Telescope detector
, is the use
of frequency dependent squeezed vacuum states of light .
This technique was, among others, proposed by Kimble et al. 
and aims for the conversion of conventional Michelson-based GW detectors into
QND interferometers, to achieve a broadband improvement of the quantum noise
limited sensitivity. However, all the
schemes proposed in have in common that they come at the expense
of substantially increased technical complexity as they require the adoption of
large scale low-loss filter cavities.A new approach which is based on performing a measurement of an
observable which is intrinsically a QND
observable, i.e. a conserved quantity, was first introduced to the field of GW
interferometry by Braginsky.
In so-called speed
meters the intention was to measure the momentum of the test masses, for which
their relative velocity was thought to be a good proxy
.

input: How does CKM construction at tree-level compare to unitarity triangle precision in terms of CP implications, and what are the differences in their approaches to achieving precise CP violation measurements?
expected_output: The construction of the CKM matrix at tree-level and the unitarity triangle approach differ in their methods to achieve precise CP violation measurements. The tree-level construction of the CKM matrix utilizes the measured values of the CKM elements, while the unitarity triangle approach employs the unitarity of the CKM matrix to constrain the parameters. In terms of CP implications, the tree-level construction is sensitive to the CP violating phase, and the unitarity triangle approach provides a framework to estimate the likely presence of CP violation in the leptonic sector. The main difference between the two approaches lies in their treatment of theoretical inputs and experimental errors, with the tree-level construction being more susceptible to New Physics effects and the unitarity triangle approach providing a more robust framework for precision measurements. Overall, both approaches are essential for understanding the CKM phenomenology and achieving precise CP violation measurements, with the unitarity triangle approach offering a more comprehensive framework for analyzing the CP implications.

matrices. Taking clue from quark mixing phenomenology, an
analogous analysis of the leptonic unitarity triangle allows an
estimate of the likely presence of CP violation in the leptonic
sector.In the last few years, several important developments have taken
place in the context of phenomenology of Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa
(CKM) matrix as well as neutrino oscillations. On the
one hand, in the case of CKM phenomenology, we have entered the
era of precision measurements of some of the CKM parameters like {{formula:fe4c4d5e-cd8f-4357-b1a8-1299f7a65ddb}} , etc.. In this context,
based on elaborate inputs including the loop dominated parameters
such as {{formula:aaf15cd5-d41c-4ca0-bc40-a0b09e93c4ed}} , {{formula:8f5b616b-abd6-4a91-9020-b18d1e42557c}} , {{formula:57206f99-66ee-4d99-9c97-d197f04a7a49}} , {{formula:98017522-fa3d-48f4-a502-f6225a2770ec}} ,
etc., known to be susceptible to effects of NP, several recent
updates of the detailed analyses - are
available which not only give insight into the CKM phenomenology
but also enable one to fix the CKM matrix. On the other hand, in
the case of neutrino oscillations, due to the solar neutrino
experiments -, atmospheric neutrino
experiments - and the reactor 
as well as accelerator based experiments, there have
been continuous improvements in the corresponding neutrino mass
square differences and mixing angles, however these are not
adequate to `construct' the Pontecorvo-Maki-Nakagata-Saki (PMNS)
matrix without further theoretical inputs.The quark and neutrino mixing matrices are well known to be
related to their corresponding mass matrices which are formulated
at the GUT (Grand Unified Theories) scale, therefore a well
determined mixing matrix would have deep implications for the
GUTs. In the case of quarks, the relationship is fairly straight
forward, however the implications of elements of the mixing matrix
on those of mass matrix are not that direct.

The fermion masses and mixings not only provide a fertile ground
to hunt for physics beyond the SM but also pose a big challenge to
understand these from more fundamental considerations. In the
present work, attempts have been made to present a comprehensive
review of some of the aspects of fermion mixing phenomenon and
texture specific mass matrices. In the context of fermion mixings,
keeping in mind the role played by unitarity of the CKM matrix and
unitarity triangles in establishing the CKM paradigm, implications
of these on parameters like sin{{formula:bb6df59d-ad3b-4e85-bafb-54cbb9b7c558}} , {{formula:ac7573bc-b480-45ea-8f9e-739fff39088e}} and phase
{{formula:e7f9b7d0-a68a-44cc-a67d-fb2cb164f79a}} have been discussed. Interestingly, one finds that
unitarity along with precisely measured {{formula:f65a84ec-08e4-4b2b-b813-1822c4c235da}} , {{formula:915321b7-2314-4d1c-a40e-838ec5001c09}} ,
sin{{formula:4973bfbf-2212-43e4-b034-f73f53724cc6}} and angle {{formula:212b902d-1481-43e8-8687-b56947d81a77}} provides important constraints on
the CKM matrix element {{formula:c9b512c7-730c-4518-838b-5e3a294d9a2e}} and the CP violating phase
{{formula:77be798c-f418-4b07-a7e8-89271cb7f53c}} .The recent precision measurements of CKM phenomenological
parameters along with several developments in the lattice QCD
calculations of hadronic factors in the case of {{formula:d57eb69a-da29-4575-81af-5ee322f596cf}} and
the {{formula:5e874e3b-67e1-4e92-ace0-39176a8f785a}} mixings and the contribution of the long
distance effects in the {{formula:18d327c7-e2ad-4f65-97ef-4b23d55b6973}} system provide motivation to
investigate the implications of these for the CKM phenomenology.
In this context, some authors, point towards the
possibility of New Physics (NP) in these systems to the tune of
20{{formula:0dc27d91-19d4-4344-999b-18aba0785396}} or so. However, a recent analysis has made
an attempt to re-look this issue and interestingly, one finds that
both the {{formula:b0324bf7-92be-48d0-aa28-f53322e4f716}} and {{formula:67ae25b5-985c-4539-9985-27cde0df6a2f}} systems do not seem
to provide any significant clues regarding the possibility of
existence of NP and therefore, the presence of NP effects, if any,
would be less than a few percent only.The issues of unitarity of the PMNS matrix and unitarity triangles
in the leptonic sector have also been discussed in the present
work. To this end, attempts have been made to
explore the possibility of the construction of the leptonic
unitarity triangle in the modified tribimaximal scenario of
Bjorken et al. .

At present, there is clear evidence that the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix is complex, even if one allows for the presence of new physics in the {{formula:ddb3d22c-9325-45a4-94b6-740f0818a7c0}} -{{formula:7dd7859a-1126-487a-ae4c-255e874b8c44}} and {{formula:49c9f6fa-6d6f-4c2b-adbe-824facab7608}} -{{formula:c8f43ebd-818f-4de7-92c2-5064dfeec5bf}} mixings. From a theoretical point of view, the complex phase in the CKM matrix may arise from complex Yukawa couplings and/or from a relative CP-violating phase in the vacuum expectation values (VEV) of Higgs fields. In either case, one expects an entirely analogous mechanism to arise in the lepton sector, leading to leptonic CP violation (LCPV).
The discovery of neutrino oscillations provides evidence for non-vanishing neutrino masses and leptonic mixing. Therefore, it is imperative to look for possible manifestations of CP violation in leptonic interactions. The recent measurement of reactor mixing angle {{formula:90785f27-4b62-4de7-8597-c972c4f419cb}} and its subsequent refinements, along with the precision measurement of the solar and atmospheric mixing angles {{formula:6f1976e2-0636-4b06-8745-728e6a888b86}} and {{formula:af6b9cab-a212-4e6d-9fcb-daa36d63e497}} as well as of the neutrino mass squared differences have given a new impetus to the neutrino oscillation phenomenology. The observation of non-zero value of {{formula:27c201f9-c15b-492d-b24a-600756a01748}} , on the one hand, restored the parallelism between quark and lepton mixing, while, it has triggered great deal of interest in the exploration of CP violation in the leptonic sector. The search for CP violation in the leptonic sector at low energies is one of the major challenges for experimental neutrino physics. Experiments with superbeams and neutrino beams from neutrino factories have the potential to measure either directly the Dirac phase {{formula:b1c0d768-a940-4029-93b2-f6beb2547f2a}} through the observation of CP and T asymmetries or indirectly through neutrino oscillations. An alternative method is to measure the area of the unitarity triangles defined for the leptonic sector. In addition, the effects of Majorana type phases may arise in neutrinoless double beta decay ({{formula:a298899d-e193-4a0d-8ad8-4c75e641237a}} ) processes. The observation of such processes would establish the Majorana nature of neutrinos and, possibly, provide some information on the Majorana CP phases. Thus, neutrino physics provides an invaluable tool for the investigation of leptonic CP violation at low energies apart from having profound implications for the physics of the early universe. In this direction, reconstruction of neutrino mass matrix is necessary as it encodes the information of CP violation, however in the present scenario of neutrino oscillation data it is impossible to fully construct neutrino mass matrix. Therefore, several proposals have been made in the literature to restrict the form of mass matrix, .

input: What are the limitations of using auto-fit isochrones in determining age accuracy, and how do different methodologies impact the overall precision of age estimates?
expected_output: The use of auto-fit isochrones in determining age accuracy has several limitations, including the potential for stochastic effects, large color dispersion at fainter magnitudes, and photometry incompleteness at the bottom part of the color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs). Additionally, residuals from field star decontamination can also impact the accuracy of age estimates. The automatic technique used by B17 to fit isochrones to the observed CMDs may have left little space to control these effects, which could have resulted in inaccurate age estimates, particularly for older clusters. Furthermore, the presence of residual LMC red clump stars, in combination with relatively faint main sequences, could mimic the appearance of features typically seen in CMDs of clusters older than log(8.7) years, leading to incorrect age estimates. Different methodologies, such as the use of nominal reddenings and the selection of isochrones, can also impact the overall precision of age estimates, highlighting the need for careful consideration of these factors in determining the ages of star clusters.

input: What is the typical size ratio of inner disks to their parent bars in S0 galaxies, and how does this vary across different galaxy samples?
expected_output: The typical size ratio of inner disks to their parent bars in S0 galaxies is around 19% for the WIYN sample and 20% for the expanded sample. This size ratio is systematically larger compared to inner bars, which is not due to the inner disks being larger in absolute size, but rather because the parent bars of inner-disk galaxies are systematically smaller, with a median radius of 3.9 kpc, compared to the outer bars of double-barred galaxies, which have a median radius of 5.7 kpc. This difference in size ratio is statistically significant, with K-S tests indicating that inner bars and disks come from different parent populations at a 99.8% confidence level.
context:
Nonetheless, the existence of inner disks helps
to solve the problem that they themselves create, since at least in
some cases the “true” spheroidal bulge component — rounder,
kinematically hot and, in these cases, non-exponential — can be
cleanly separated from an inner disk, using unequivocal photometric
criteria. By effecting such a separation for the present galaxies we
show that past analyses have dramatically overestimated their bulge
sizes. For NGC 3945 we find that the true bulge is astonishingly
small: its half-light radius is just over 100 pc, in a galaxy with a
bar of radial length 5 kpc, and an outer ring of radius 14 kpc; the
bulge accounts for only {{formula:ec77ad5c-eb52-48f6-bef2-dbdc7c066b76}} % of the total luminosity, a figure
more typical of Sc galaxies than of S0 galaxies. In NGC 2787, the
bulge is larger (half-light radius {{formula:2de3c28d-0b4c-444b-a4e5-7368c845c3de}} pc and {{formula:61b3eb31-1f23-4493-87b1-fb94c12280d1}} % of the
total luminosity), but the presence of the inner disk produces a
radial surface-brightness profile which can lead one to overestimate
the bulge size by factors of 2–5.

Here, our classification is based purely on orientation: an elliptical
structure (within a large bar) which is aligned to within 10 of
the galaxy's outer disk is called an inner disk, as long as unsharp
masking does not show it to be, e.g., a nuclear ring instead.
Clearly, this class will include at least some inner bars with chance
alignments, along with unresolved nuclear rings and possibly flattened
inner bulges. However, there are several pieces of evidence
indicating that our inner disks form a physically distinct class.In the WIYN sample, inner disks are as common as inner bars in S0
galaxies, but practically absent in later Hubble types: 35% of the S0
galaxies had an inner disk, while we found one inner disk in an S0/a
galaxy and none in Sa galaxies. This contrasts strongly with inner
bars, which are equally common for S0, S0/a, and Sa galaxies. Inner
disks are also too common for them all to be chance
alignments of randomly oriented inner bars. Finally, inner disks are
systematically larger with respect to their parent bars (median size =
19% for WIYN sample, 20% for expanded sample); K-S tests indicate

input: Do isolation measures actually reduce COVID-19 transmission rates in densely populated areas, and can their effectiveness be improved by combining them with other public health interventions?
expected_output: Isolation measures have been shown to reduce COVID-19 transmission rates in densely populated areas. According to the context, simulations demonstrate the dampening effect of isolation on the dissemination of the disease. Additionally, the results of a study on the Brazilian epidemic suggest that keeping current isolation levels can lead to a prolonged propagation of the disease, but with a slower rate of new cases and deaths. The context also highlights the importance of combining isolation measures with other public health interventions, such as flexible approaches to regional assignments and increased testing, to improve their effectiveness. Furthermore, the use of visualization metaphors and graph-theoretical tools can help analyze the evolution of the pandemic and identify areas where isolation measures can be most effective. Overall, the evidence suggests that isolation measures can be an effective tool in reducing COVID-19 transmission rates in densely populated areas, particularly when combined with other public health interventions.
context: Visual analytics techniques help discover patterns that would be difficult to perceive by looking only at raw data. In this work, we employed visualization metaphors to analyze the evolution of the number of cases of COVID-19 in the São Paulo state, Brazil. Our methodology consists of visualizing the dissemination based on time windows and contrasting the number of cases in the periods of analyses with the cities' isolation indices.Throughout several analyses, we show how our visualization design helps analyze a city's situation according to the number of cases in a time window and its neighborhood situation. We show that our methodology emphasizes how the isolation index benefit cities regarding the dissemination, even when these cities are part of critical neighborhoods in the sense of the number of cases.We hope that decision-makers can use our methodology to monitor the evaluation of the number of cases in cities and neighborhoods to respond to dissemination risks quickly.

The aim of this paper is to analyse the evolution of the COVID-19 pandemic in
Rio Grande do Sul by applying graph-theoretical tools, particularly spectral
clustering techniques, on weighted graphs defined on the set of 167
municipalities in the state with population 10,000 or more, which are based on
data provided by government agencies and other sources. To respond to this
outbreak, the state has adopted a system by which pre-determined regions are
assigned flags on a weekly basis, and different measures go into effect
according to the flag assigned. Our results suggest that considering a flexible
approach to the regions themselves might be a useful additional tool to give
more leeway to cities with lower incidence rates, while keeping the focus on
public safety. Moreover, simulations show the dampening effect of isolation on
the dissemination of the disease.

This work presents a new approach for the modeling of the COVID-19 epidemic dynamics based on multi-layer complex networks. Each node represents a person, and edges are social interactions divided into 6 layers: home, work, transports, schools, religions, and random relations. Each layer has its own characteristics based on how people usually interact in that activity. The propagation is performed using an agent-based technique, a modification of the SIR model, where weights represent the infection probability that varies depending on the layers and the groups the node interacts, scaled by a {{formula:11da54db-8543-4121-8626-bafe68352012}} term that controls the chances of infection. The network structure is built based on demographic statistics of a given country, region, or city, and the propagation simulation is performed at time iterations, that represent days. Here, we studied in depth the case of the Brazilian epidemic considering its population properties and also specific events, such as when the first isolation measures were taken, and the impacts of future actions.Brazil is a large and populated country with a wide variety of geographical location types, climates, and it also has a lengthy border with other countries to the west. It is a challenging setting for any epidemiological study. Here we consider an average over all the country population, as we adjust the model output to match some statistics of the epidemic official reports. Brazil is performing fewer tests in comparison to other countries at the same epidemic scale, however, it is known that testing for infection is always limited, either due to the low number of tests or to the velocity of infections which the testing procedure cannot keep up to. We then considered that only hospitalization cases and {{formula:d4352988-8229-4469-8228-dfa91d9182e9}} of the mild cases are diagnosed. Asymptomatic cases are not diagnosed and keep acting normally in the network, considering the active layers. Regarding the isolation of infected nodes, we take some optimistic assumptions: Mild cases (even those not diagnosed) are aware of its symptoms and isolate themselves at home. Severe and critical cases are eventually hospitalized, and then fully isolated from the network (removal of all its edges).Under the described scenario, the network starts with all its layers and {{formula:658c2fd2-5a1f-4afe-953e-010bdfe8a97b}} , representing that people are aware of the virus since the beginning (even before isolation measures). After 27 days of the first confirmed case, the first isolation measures are taken where schools and religious activities are stopped and work and transports keep functioning at {{formula:fc2bf51a-e5f9-4610-8fb6-5e03e09ada01}} of the initial scale (achieved further reducing the {{formula:3596fd4c-28db-4ba3-b592-d1040ca68c21}} term). Different actions are then considered after 90 days of the first case: keep the current isolation levels, increase isolation, end isolation returning all activities to {{formula:773e3e02-d4f6-400d-ab8b-d411d1b2d840}} , or returning only the work activities. The results show that keeping approximately the current isolation levels results in a prolonged propagation, as we are near the estimated peak (around June 5) with an average of 11,000 daily new cases and 1900 daily new deaths, and an average of 946,830 diagnosed cases (up to 3,6 million infected) and 149,438 deaths until the end of the year. In this scenario, hospitals may exceed its maximum capacity around June 11, but the efficient implementation of new ICU beds and good logistic management of patients may still keep the situation under control.

input: What causes PMMH log-likelihood variance to exceed 1 in certain models, and how do different methodologies contribute to this phenomenon?
expected_output: The PMMH log-likelihood variance exceeds 1 in certain models due to the sensitivity of the PMMH method to the size of the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood. In many problems, it is computationally demanding to ensure that the variance of the log of the estimated likelihood is around 1, which can lead to a deterioration in the performance of the PMMH method. The use of a large number of particles, such as 2000, can help to obtain an unbiased estimate of the likelihood, but this can be computationally expensive. The correlated PMMH approach, which correlates the pseudo-random numbers used in estimating the likelihood at the current and proposed values of the Markov chain, can help to reduce the variance of the log-likelihood and improve the performance of the PMMH method. Additionally, the use of different methodologies, such as the AISIL-PG and AISIL-HMC methods, can also contribute to the phenomenon of exceeding 1, as these methods may require more tuning and can be more sensitive to the choice of parameters, such as the number of particles and leapfrog steps.

According to the context, the numerical solutions of the 3D axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations were obtained using a specific initial condition, which suggests that the choice of initial condition can impact the behavior of the solution. Furthermore, the 1D model, which preserves some essential nonlinear structure of the original 3D axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations, plays a critical role in stabilizing the solution for large times, although the same nonlinearity can lead to large dynamic growth for early times. This implies that the initial conditions can have significant implications on the overall behavior of the solutions, particularly in terms of stability and growth, across different fluid dynamics scenarios. Additionally, the use of the method of multi-scale matched asymptotic expansion to construct an approximate solution of the Navier-Stokes equations highlights the importance of considering the initial conditions in the analysis of nearly singular solutions. Overall, the initial conditions can have a profound impact on the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations' solutions, and their influence should be carefully considered in various fluid dynamics scenarios.
