input: How does the accuracy of fisheye cameras compare to that of pinhole cameras in various lighting conditions, and what are the key differences in their performance across different applications?
expected_output: The accuracy of fisheye cameras compared to pinhole cameras in various lighting conditions is not explicitly stated in the context, but it is mentioned that object detection on panoramic images, such as those from fisheye cameras, is a less well-studied topic than its pinhole counterpart. The context highlights the challenges of adapting object detection models to fisheye imagery due to the oriented and radially distorted objects, and explores alternative representations for standard bounding boxes to improve accuracy. In terms of key differences in performance, fisheye cameras are shown to require specialized models and techniques, such as curved boxes, oriented boxes, ellipses, and polygons, to achieve reasonable tradeoffs between model complexity and accuracy. Additionally, the context notes that the performance of fisheye cameras can be improved by incorporating geometric priors into the loss function and using vehicle motion awareness, but a direct comparison to pinhole cameras in various lighting conditions is not provided. Overall, the context suggests that fisheye cameras have unique challenges and requirements that differ from those of pinhole cameras, particularly in applications such as autonomous driving and object detection.
context: In this paper, we introduced a new moving object detection dataset for fisheye cameras. Firstly, we showed that the model trained on rectilinear KITTI dataset does not generalize well for fisheye images. We designed an efficient architecture for moving object segmentation and provided baseline experiments. We also tested different training and augmentation techniques to improve accuracy. We will make an improved version of the dataset public in order to encourage further research. In future work, we plan to incorporate geometric priors into the loss function to improve accuracy.

In this paper, we proposed a vehicle motion aware moving object detection. We demonstrated significant improvements over the baseline by using vehicle motion on KITTI_MoSeg _Extended dataset.
Majority of this dataset comprises of the vehicle going in a straight line with a standard urban driving velocity and we expect larger improvements on a more diverse ego-motion dataset. We perform a comparative study on different types of network architectures and fusion mechanisms to find the best model which achieves state-of-the-art results. Given the emergence of low-cost IMU sensors for commercial deployment, we hope that our work encourages further research in using vehicle motion for other tasks including tracking and depth estimation.

Object detection on panoramic images is a topic that is also less well-studied than its pinhole counterpart within the literature. One concept that has been researched to adapt object detection models to fisheye imagery, which frequently has oriented and radially distorted objects, is alternative representations for standard bounding boxes.   explored the usage of curved boxes, oriented boxes, ellipses, and polygons. YOLOv3  was adapted and modified to output these different representations. The results show that 24-sided polygons achieved the most reasonable tradeoffs between model complexity and accuracy. Further analysis also reports no drops in inference speed when increasing the number of vertices. Alternatively,   proposed a simple framework for oriented box representation by gliding each vertex of the original horizontal box on its corresponding side to get more accurate coverage of the detected object and demonstrated the method's effectiveness in object detection on aerial images, texts, and pedestrians in fisheye images. presented a localization method by leveraging top-view fisheye images from a UAV and altitude data. The proposed framework first involves acquiring pixel positions of objects using an object detection model implemented based on the RetinaNet model  with MobileNet  backbone for more efficient computing. Then, by fusing the camera's parameter and height data from other sensors, a series of coordinate transforms is performed to obtain the object's position in world coordinates.In addition, some public fisheye image datasets were published to facilitate the development of this field of research. Most noticeable is the Woodscape dataset  for autonomous driving, comprising over 100,000 images from four surrounding cameras. Later, in 2022, the KITTI-360 dataset  was released as a successor to the popular KITTI dataset . It expanded on the original work with more data for suburban driving from multiple sensor units, including two 180 fisheye cameras on each side of the station wagon.

input: What is the process for adapting TTRS to open-source software, and how can TTRC's approach be applied to achieve this adaptation?
expected_output: The process for adapting Time To Restore Service (TTRS) to open-source software involves modifying the metric to Time To Repair Code (TTRC), which measures the time it takes to release a new version of the code that includes changes that correct bugs. To achieve this adaptation, the TTRC approach can be applied by calculating the time difference between the moment a bug issue is raised and the moment the changes that solve the bug are released in a new version of the code. This is done by defining a formula that sums up the time differences for each bug and then dividing by the total number of bugs reported during a period of time. The result is the mean time to repair code, which can be used to evaluate the stability of open-source software projects. Additionally, the standard deviation of the time to repair code can be calculated to reflect the variations in the time it takes to solve different bugs, providing further insight into the project's stability.

In the context of the DORA reports, Time To Restore Service is a metric used to measure stability. It measures how long it typically takes to restore service after an bug or defect that impacts users.However, in OSS projects, this metric is not directly applicable as there is no central operations service where the software is deployed and the team is responsible for maintaining the quality of the service. Instead, OSS projects release versions of the software that can be used by third parties. Therefore, the Time To Restore Service metric in OSS projects is adapted to the Time To Repair Code, which refers to the time it takes to release a new version of the code that includes changes that correct bugs.In order to measure this metric we tried to develop an approximation based on the information we could retrieve from GitHub. The time it takes to repair a bug would be the time passed between the moment in which the bug issue is raised and the moment in which the changes that solve that bug are released in a new version of the code. We define the following formula:m_{r} = \cfrac{\mathop {\mmlmultiscripts{\sum {i=0}{n_{e}}}}\limits t_{r}-t_{e_{i}}}{n_{e}}Being t_{r} the moment in which the changes that solve the bug are released, t_{e_{i}} the moment in which the team is notified about the bug (the issue reporting the bug is opened), n_{e} the number of bugs that users reported in a period of time and lead to changes in the code and m_{r} the time to repair code.In the case of not having any changes that solve bugs made to the code during the measuring period, this metric could not be calculated because of lack of data.In this metric, the standard deviation reflects the variations in the time it takes to solve bugs. A high standard deviation represents large variations, meaning that the time it takes to solve different bugs varies. A low standard deviation represents a little variation in the time it takes to solve different bugs. We propose the following formula:d_{m} = \sqrt{\cfrac{\mathop {\mmlmultiscripts{\sum {i=0}{n_{e}}}}\limits t_{md_{i}}-m_{md}}{n_{e}}}Being t_{md_{i}} the time it takes to solve a bug (calculated before for the Time To Repair Code as t_{r} - t_{e_{i}}),

input: What are the limitations of using scale hierarchies to approximate metrics near horizons, and how do different approaches perform in practice?
expected_output: The limitations of using scale hierarchies to approximate metrics near horizons are rooted in the assumption of a separation of scales between the characteristic scale of the perturbations and some intrinsic microscopic scale. This assumption is crucial for the derivation of the Navier-Stokes equations and the membrane equations, which are used to describe the behavior of fluids near horizons. However, in practice, the performance of different approaches can vary significantly depending on the specific context and the choice of parameters. For instance, the correlation length of a fluid near a horizon can scale as the inverse of the Hawking temperature, which can lead to significant deviations from the expected behavior if not properly accounted for. Furthermore, the definition of the near-horizon region and the choice of the outer boundary can also affect the accuracy of the approximations. In general, the use of scale hierarchies to approximate metrics near horizons requires careful consideration of the underlying assumptions and the potential limitations of the approach.

input: Does ResNet-MLP actually improve palm image classification compared to traditional convolutional neural networks, and what are the key factors contributing to its potential success or failure in this application?
expected_output: ResNet-MLP has the potential to improve palm image classification compared to traditional convolutional neural networks due to its ability to capture complex patterns in data by introducing non-linearity through its multi-layer perceptron (MLP) architecture. The key factors contributing to its potential success include the incorporation of batch normalization layers, which enhance the model's ability to learn from ResNet's feature vectors and map them to the appropriate class labels. Additionally, the use of layer normalization and the ReLU nonlinear activation function throughout the training process can also contribute to its success. However, the actual improvement of ResNet-MLP over traditional convolutional neural networks in palm image classification depends on various factors, including the specific architecture and parameters of the model, the quality of the training data, and the complexity of the classification task. The replacement of conventional convolutional layers with MLP layers, denoted as ResNet-MLP-g, and the composition of ResNet-MLP-g from multiple ResNet-MLP-s modules, each consisting of multiple fully connected layers, are also crucial factors that can impact the performance of ResNet-MLP in palm image classification.
context: To classify the palm images based on the extracted features from ResNet layers, PalmProbNet employs an MLP that can capture complex patterns in data by introducing non-linearity . input: What are the effects of Type Ia Supernovae on star formation in young globular clusters, and how do these effects vary across different astrophysical environments?
expected_output: The effects of Type Ia Supernovae on star formation in young globular clusters are significant, but vary depending on the ambient gas density. In low-density environments, Type Ia Supernovae can severely limit star formation by confining gas far from the cluster center, whereas in high-density environments, they have only mild effects on star formation and helium enrichment. The high-density model shows that the pristine gas slows the SN bubble expansion, leading to a second generation of stars with very modest helium enrichment. Additionally, the iron distribution of the second generation stars is significantly affected by the presence of Type Ia Supernovae, resulting in a significant iron enrichment. The effects of Type Ia Supernovae also depend on the delay times for their onset, with longer delay times needed in low-density models to increase the contribution of pristine gas and dilution. Overall, the impact of Type Ia Supernovae on star formation in young globular clusters is complex and sensitive to the astrophysical environment.
context:
Their results indicate that type Ia SNe are able to severely limit SF only assuming an ambient gas density of {{formula:715a849f-eeb7-4cea-8dca-3d96808834fb}} g cm{{formula:d721d3ba-a2e5-4b93-8110-8a44ad7588d0}} ,
whereas their higher-density case ( {{formula:55c06931-df89-4b6c-b567-e291eeadd4d2}} g cm{{formula:b2100dcd-e70b-4de7-a0c4-c62f1dc3b777}} ) is weakly affected by SN explosions, with a final SG mass similar
to the one obtained without SNe Ia.
In the future, it will be very important to extend the study of to cluster of different masses, like the ones considered
in this paper, in order to improve our still limited understanding of the effects of discrete feedback sources on the ISM and, most of all,
to probe the effects of different numbers of SNe explosions on mass accretion and on star formation in young GCs.

The infall of pristine gas starts before the SN explosions, so some of it is accreted by the system and dilutes the AGB ejecta. At variance with the previous model, not all the stars show an extreme helium enrichment; a small fraction of stars display an intermediate helium enrichment as a result of a dilution and are spatially less concentrated than the extreme
population. The accretion of pristine gas continues for about 5 Myr but, eventually, Type Ia SNe confine the gas far from the cluster centre as it happened in the model without delay. However, dilution is still too low and the spread in helium between the two generations is still much larger than the observed values. Therefore, longer delay times for the onset of Type Ia SNe are needed by the low density models in order to increase the contribution of the pristine gas and therefore the extent of dilution.

In the high-density model, Type Ia SNe have only mild effects both on the SFR evolution and on the helium enrichment. The final SG mass is only 1.2 times smaller than without Type Ia SNe. The higher density assumed for the pristine gas prevents Type Ia from confining it in the cluster outer regions, as found in the low-density models. In this model, the pristine gas slows the SN bubble expansion decreasing the growth of their filling factor. In this case an accretion column is present, even though it is continuously perturbed by SN explosions. The overall continuous accretion of gas leads to a SG dominated by stars with very modest helium enrichment ({{formula:939059be-9bd7-44de-9ef5-eade18fef9e7}} ), similarly to what is obtained without Type Ia SNe. On the contrary, the SG iron distribution is significantly affected by the presence of Type Ia SNe. Since their bubbles are confined by the infalling gas, most of the iron released during their explosions is retained by the system and then recycled to form new stars which show a significant iron enrichment. The mean [Fe/H] ratio of SG stars is, in fact, equal to [Fe/H]{{formula:155bc956-7009-46f5-957b-4e09b83fe7b9}} dex. Assuming that, after the subsequent evolution, SG stars account for {{formula:5268e5f4-cb7a-4ae2-9a2b-b2dd7249b19d}} of the whole cluster, we derive an internal iron dispersion of {{formula:d10ab508-77d0-466e-9315-98ecceb56427}} , in good agreement with the typical spread observed in Type II GCs.

No substantial difference has been found between the standard high-density model and the one with a delayed cooling meaning that, overall, the impact of Type Ia SNe is not artificially suppressed by cooling.It has to be noted that in all our simulations we do not include ionizing feedback from SG stars which could lead to a steeper decrease of the SFR . Massive stars belonging to the SG, if any, should contribute to heat up the ISM further, reducing the amount of gas eligible for star formation. However, the SG formation is supposed to take place in an environment already crowded by the FG stars, a scenario in which the SF process is still unexplored .

We find that, unless the gas density around SNe Ia is too low
({{formula:62966abf-5ec8-4c3f-8bae-c0ea3f2df508}} cm{{formula:46d148f7-4695-464c-8fce-3ec457a2aabd}} ), the newly formed grains are
almost completely destroyed in the shocked gas in the course of their
injection into the ISM.
Even if the asymmetric effect of explosion is taken into account,
SNe Ia is likely to be poor producers of interstellar dust.
However, SNe Ia are major production factories of heavy elements which
will be available for the subsequent growth of the pre-existing grains
through accretion onto their surface in the dense molecular clouds.We thank R. Kotak and Y. Kamiya for the useful comments.
We are grateful to the anonymous referee for critical comments
that are useful for improving the manuscript.

input: How does Gini impurity compare to Entropy impurity in terms of their effectiveness in decision tree splitting across different datasets and algorithms?
expected_output: Gini impurity and Entropy impurity are two of the most commonly used impurity measures in decision tree splitting, and their effectiveness can vary across different datasets and algorithms. In general, both measures are effective in guiding the decision tree splitting process, but they have different properties that can make one more suitable than the other in certain situations. The Gini impurity measure is used in the CART package, while the Entropy impurity measure is used in the C4.5 decision tree inducer. Research has shown that the choice of impurity measure can affect the performance of the decision tree, with some studies suggesting that Entropy impurity can lead to more accurate classifications, while others have found that Gini impurity can result in more efficient tree construction. Ultimately, the choice of impurity measure depends on the specific characteristics of the dataset and the goals of the analysis.

Decision Trees and Random Forests are among the most popular
methods for classification tasks.
It is widely known that decision trees, specially small ones, are easy to interpret
while random forest usually yield
to more stable/accurate classifications.A key decision during the construction of these structures
is the selection of the attribute that is used for branching at each node.
The standard approach for this selection is to
evaluate the ability of each attribute to generate 'pure' partitions, that is, partitions in which each branch is very homogeneous with respect to the class distribution
of its examples. To measure how impure each branch is, impurity measures are often employed.
An impurity measure maps a vector {{formula:608b054c-f0c8-4716-8465-42e93f3c53d3}} , counting how many examples of each class we have in a node (branch), into a non-negative scalar In the original definition an impurity measure maps a vector

{{formula:ba214521-f779-4b54-8038-6988a96a9926}}which is

{{formula:f850b00c-aa03-4d09-bfcd-9f759d34f226}}that along with its variants is used in the C4.5 decision tree inducer

for the attribute values that induces a partition of the set of examples with minimum weighted impurity, where the weights are given by the number of examples that lie into
each of the branches.Here, we discuss connections between the problem of
computing the partition with minimum weighted Gini and the {{formula:77076cc4-2d15-4e48-8921-2003e69873b5}} -means clustering problem.

input: What is the process for applying wavelength and flat-field calibrations to grism spectra in a way that ensures accurate and reliable results across different observational settings?
expected_output: The process for applying wavelength and flat-field calibrations to grism spectra involves several steps to ensure accurate and reliable results. First, the wavelengths in the grism spectrum are calculated using coefficients recommended by STScI, with modifications as needed to achieve optimal agreement between the observed spectra and known profiles. The coefficients are varied by up to 10% through trial-and-error to obtain good consistency of the grism response and accounting of stellar absorption lines. Additionally, a wavelength-dependent flat field calibration is applied as recommended by STScI, which is a function of where each target's spectrum falls on the detector and must be done at the user stage of data analysis. However, if the stellar spectra are fixed on the detector during each visit and jitter and drift in wavelength are negligible, flat-fielding may not be necessary. The entire analysis can be repeated without the flat-fielding step to verify consistent results, and this step is prudent in cases where wavelength jitter in spatial scan mode can be larger than in non-scanned observations. Overall, the application of wavelength and flat-field calibrations requires careful consideration of the observational settings and the specific characteristics of the data to ensure accurate and reliable results.
context:
Our analysis started with the images provided by the STScI pipeline.
These are corrected with bias subtraction,
dark current subtraction after scaling to individual
exposure times, and converted from digital units to electrons scaling by
the detector gain. Retrievals from the STSci archive were made
only after final biases and darks were available.These images are not flat-fielded for grism data.
For the very similar GO/DD-10441 observations of TrES-1 (Brown et al., in preparation)
in which HRC grism spectra at high S/N were obtained at nearly
the same place on the detector, but without the complication
of saturation and bleeding, it was found that use of a wavelength-dependent
flat field provided no benefit.
Facing the extra complication here of saturated data and
needing to take into account the flat fields as a function
only of electron origination, not current location, we simply
have not applied flat fields for these data.
For our purposes of deriving differential time series
over time, in which all of the spectra have been taken at
nominally the same pointing, and for which the extractions
are averaged over a large domain (over 5000 pixels for the global first
order spectrum extraction), we would not expect
much sensitivity to flat fielding errors. If there were
no motion of the spectra relative to the detector as a
result of HST guiding errors, there should be no need to
flat field. These guiding errors, while not zero, are
quite small ({{formula:12baf452-a0db-49e8-90a5-598b0329c185}} pixel), and at a later step we decorrelate with
vectors that remove any small noise resulting from lack
of flat fielding.

We began our treatment of the data using the calibrated output from
the STScI data processing pipeline. The pipeline reduction consists of
dark current removal on a read-by-read basis, linearization, bad pixel
masking, and cosmic ray rejection. At this stage the data remain in
the format of two dimensional, single frame images for each
exposure. The principal elements of the reduction process that are
accomplished by the pipeline to this point are the first order
bias and dark subtraction, linearization and CR rejection. Our
subsequent processing improves on the bias and dark
subtraction, bad pixel masking and more complete rejection of particle
events. The calibrated grism exposures have not been corrected for the
flat field response and have not had the sky background removed. The
flat-field response is a function of wavelength for each pixel and so
depends on the location of each object, and will not be the same for
the object and the sky. The flat-field correction is applied during
the 1-D spectral extraction.We constructed a median sky frame for the G141 grism by combining the
calibrated exposures for approximately 200 frames, covering 80
independent positions on the sky. We rejected observations made at
low galactic latitudes as well as those centered on bright objects or
crowded fields. This produced a high signal-to-noise uncorrected sky
frame for use in the sky subtraction for each exposure. The observed
background rates vary significantly from frame-to-frame depending on
the ecliptic latitude and longitude. We subtracted a scaled version of
the median sky from each calibrated 2-D spectral frame. The optimal
scaling for the sky was found by minimizing the RMS noise in two
object-free regions of each frame. Very low-spatial frequency
structure remained in the background of many frames, primarily due to
the shading effect in the NICMOS arrays. We removed a low order
surface from each frame. This surface was derived from a second order
polynomial fit to an intermediate image constructed from the median of
each column. This surface fitting was carried out separately in each
quadrant of the detector, allowing us to remove small
quadrant-to-quadrant bias variations. The individual sky subtracted
and shading corrected frames were then shifted into registration,
using offsets derived from the accompanying direct images. The
registered 2D spectra were then averaged with a bad pixel mask and
{{formula:f554c8c7-5bc8-41c4-9843-3784eb557467}} clipping applied to remove hot pixels and residual cosmic
rays.The direct images that are used to calibrated the extracted one
dimensional spectra were processed and combined using the same
techniques as above, but without the sky subtraction and low order
surface fitting correction steps.

Following the initial data processing described above, we apply
wavelength and flat-field calibrations. Each visit includes an
undispersed image of the star, and the wavelengths in the grism
spectrum are reliably fixed relative to the position of the undispersed
image. We calculate those wavelengths using coefficients recommended
by STScI , with some modifications. found that the
original recommended coefficients did not produce optimal agreement
between the overall profile of the grism response in observed spectra
when compared to the known profile of that response, and also did not
give exact agreement with the known wavelengths of stellar absorption
lines. varied the coefficients by up to 10% by
trial-and-error, to achieve optimal agreement. We have used the
 coefficients, and we obtain good consistency of the
grism response, and good accounting of stellar absorption lines (e.g.,
Paschen-beta, see below).In addition to wavelength calibration, we apply the wavelength-dependent flat field calibration as recommended by STScI.
Note that flat-fielding is not included in STScI pipeline
processing, even for the files of non-spatial-scan data,
because it is a function of where each target's spectrum happens to fall on
the detector, and must be done at the user stage of data analysis. To
the extent that the stellar spectra were fixed on the detector during
each visit, and jitter and drift in wavelength were negligible,
flat-fielding would not be needed in our analysis. In that (ideal)
case, we would not apply the flat-fielding step, since it has been our
experience that the more the data are processed, the more difficult it
becomes to achieve photon-limited results. However, wavelength jitter
in spatial scan mode can be larger than in non-scanned observations,
so the flat-fielding step of the analysis is prudent. However, we
have repeated the entire analysis of this paper without the
flat-fielding step, and we find consistent results in the two cases.

input: What are the limitations of applying diamagnetic inequalities to calculate grand partition functions in large-limit qubit systems, and how do these limitations impact the accuracy of the results?
expected_output: The limitations of applying diamagnetic inequalities to calculate grand partition functions in large-limit qubit systems stem from the assumptions and approximations inherent in the inequalities themselves. In the context of large-limit qubit systems, the diamagnetic inequality provides a bound for the logarithm of the ratio of the grand partition functions, but its accuracy may be impacted by the complexity of the system and the specific conditions under which the inequality is applied. Furthermore, the inequality is typically used in conjunction with numerical results, which may introduce additional limitations and uncertainties. As a result, the accuracy of the results obtained using diamagnetic inequalities in large-limit qubit systems may be affected by the interplay between the theoretical bounds and the numerical approximations, potentially leading to limitations in the precision and reliability of the calculated grand partition functions.

input: What is the correlation between Hα emission and star formation timescales across different galaxy types?
expected_output: The Hα emission is a tracer of recent star formation, with star formation timescales of approximately 10 Myr, which is the typical lifetime of young and massive O- and B-type stars. This correlation holds across different galaxy types, as Hα emission is used to estimate star formation rates (SFRs) in various galaxies, including star-forming, post-starburst, and green valley galaxies. The use of the Baldwin, Phillips & Terlevich (BPT) emission line diagnostic diagram helps to identify purely star-forming regions within galaxies, ensuring that the Hα emission is not contaminated by other ionization sources, such as active galactic nuclei (AGN). Overall, the Hα emission is a reliable indicator of recent star formation activity, allowing for the investigation of star formation timescales and scaling relations across different galaxy types.
context:
For galaxies with well-detected emission lines, we use the H\alpha line to estimate SFRs. H\alpha emission traces hydrogen ionized by a variety of sources including star formation, active galactic nuclei (AGN), and shocks. Ionized hydrogen traced by stars roughly translates to star formation timescales of \sim 10 Myr (e.g., ), i.e., the typical lifetimes of the young and massive O- and B-type stars. As such, H\alpha emission is a recent star formation tracer. In order to ensure that the H\alpha emission is devoid of contamination from other ionization sources (AGN in particular), we use the Baldwin, Phillips & Terlevich (BPT; ) emission line diagnostic diagram to identify purely star-forming spaxels within galaxies. For the BPT diagram, shown in Figure REF , we use the line ratios [OIII]\lambda 5007/H\beta and [NII]\lambda 6584/H\alpha , and require all 4 emission lines to have S/N \ge 3 for a spaxel to be used in the analysis. However, we observe spaxels with good detection (i.e., S/N \ge 3) in H\alpha but weak (i.e., S/N < 3) signal in [NII]\lambda 6584, which suggests that we may be missing out on additional SF. To recover as many star-forming spaxels as possible, we take 3 times the error as an upper limit of the [NII]\lambda 6584 flux for spaxels with S/N < 3 in [NII]\lambda 6584. We then plot the spaxels with upper limits on the BPT diagram, where we include those that fall in the SF region, whereas those that fall in the composite or AGN regions are excluded entirely from the analysis due to concerns of noise contamination (e.g., this method often results in spaxels in the outskirts being classified as AGN). This results in a total of 16,511 spaxels, where 12,882 (3,055 being upper limits) of them are classified as star-forming. We use the H\alpha emission line to measure SFRs for the 12,882 spaxels classified as star-forming.
[Figure: BPT diagram for a total of 16,511 spaxels that satisfy either one of the following conditions: (1) S/N \ge 3 in all 4 emission lines - [OIII]\lambda 5007, H\beta , [NII]\lambda 6584, and H\alpha , or (2) S/N \ge 3 in all except for [NII] and falls in the SF region. 3,055 (\sim 24 per cent) of the spaxels fall under the second category. Blue denotes the star-forming spaxels, green the composite, and red the AGN. The theoretical and empirical lines from (solid) and (dashed), respectively, are used to classify spaxels into different regions on the BPT diagram.]We correct H\alpha flux maps for dust extinction with the Balmer decrement, i.e., the H\alpha /H\beta flux ratio. We first correct for foreground extinction due to the Milky Way using the E(B - V) values from .

We choose spaxels with S/N>2 in all emission lines, H{{formula:8d52ebae-c371-44cd-9876-4f962c435a90}} , H{{formula:76042832-0f5f-454a-9769-0df5153e6e1b}} , [OIII]{{formula:0879d240-df86-420f-9fab-8418b0bb1216}} 5007, [NII]{{formula:12517899-c3dc-41cc-9a71-7aebb71bf4d4}} 6584, [SII]{{formula:973baaff-4067-4cdf-8847-f51760147b22}} 6717,31 and CO(1-0). This enables us to maximise the number of spaxels available for analysis. We test the stability of the results by applying higher signal to noise cuts, and find no significant differences.
We also only select spaxels with a H{{formula:d4ff8e32-499f-4632-bd78-9724bc909a73}} equivalent width greater than 6 Angstroms (EW(H{{formula:837cd08b-110d-443a-9eaf-91f2d71ce4e5}} )>6Å) to minimise possible contamination from diffuse ionised gas. We note that this selection tends to avoid spaxels with low sSFR, relative to the resolved Star Forming Main Sequence, however this is acceptable in this analysis as our focus is to investigate the scaling relations on the Main Sequences, and in particular the origin of the rSFMS.As we are investigating the scaling relations for star forming regions we need to separate them from the other regions of the galaxies. In addition to the EW constraint discussed above,
star forming regions are selected using the [NII]–BPT diagram , with the dividing line for star forming regions. The specific BPT requirement is also needed to determine the metallicity (as metallicity diagnostics are well calibrated only for star forming regions), which will be required when using the metallicity-dependent CO conversion factor. Note that these criteria select HII regions, i.e. star forming spaxels, regardless of the classification of the parent galaxy they belonged to, e.g. we are also selecting SF spaxels in Green Valley galaxies (as well as in starburst galaxies).The flux of nebular emission lines are corrected for dust extinction by
using the extinction curve, with {{formula:1db9b805-3cbc-420e-ac98-f296ef9fe201}} , and the Balmer decrement {{formula:dc3dc357-a7c5-42c9-b063-7448d59f935a}} to estimate the dust reddening (assuming an intrinsic ratio of 2.86, corresponding to case B recombination, and a temperature of {{formula:e7a81405-9d9e-41d1-b27d-68d38b1624a5}} K).

H\alpha is a relatively good SFR indicator in the post-starburst phase, because it traces a short star formation timescale (i.e., that associated with short-lived massive stars) and dust attenuation and AGN effects can be modeled and removed.Here we convert the H\alpha fluxes from the MPA-JHU catalogs to SFR following and We do not use the SFR measurements provided by the MPA-JHU catalogs, because, for
non-star forming galaxies on the BPT diagram, including most post-starburst galaxies,
they are derived from the D4000 index
and the relation between D4000 and specific SFR (sSFR).
D4000-traced SFRs may not be calibrated accurately for post-starburst galaxies, given that the D4000-sSFR relation is sensitive to the star formation history..
We use the L_{\mathrm {H \alpha }}-SFR relation from . We estimate the amount of internal dust extinction from the observed Balmer decrement, H\alpha /H\beta . Assuming that the hydrogen nebular emission follows Case B recombination, the intrinsic Balmer flux ratio (\mathrm {H\alpha /H\beta })_0=2.86 for T_e=10^4 K. We adopt the reddening curve of . When the H\beta line flux is negative in the MPA-JHU catalogs, we assume the mean value of E(B-V) from the other post-starburst galaxies. The mean attenuation is A_V=0.92 mag.Following the methodology from , we correct for a potential underlying AGN contribution to the H\alpha flux and thus to the derived SFR. We calculate the emission-line ratios [\mbox{O\,\textsc {iii}}]/H\beta and [\mbox{N\,\textsc {ii}}]/H\alpha of our post-starburst galaxies, place them on the BPT diagram, and determine the likely AGN contributions to their H\alpha luminosity. For 230 post-starbursts with [\mbox{O\,\textsc {iii}}], [\mbox{N\,\textsc {ii}}], and H\alpha signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) < 3, we do not have a reliable AGN correction, so we do not measure their SFRs. We do not set a S/N constraint on the H\beta line, as it is not usually well-detected in our post-starburst galaxies. For the case of negative H\beta line flux, we use its 1\sigma flux upper limit to determine the corresponding 1\sigma upper limit for the AGN correction to the SFR.
When a negative correction factor is derived, if the corresponding 1\sigma upper limit is positive, we use this upper limit to determine the SFR 1\sigma upper limit; otherwise, we do not measure the SFR.We then correct for the SDSS fiber aperture using the ratio of the global SFR to the SFR within the SDSS fiber (SFR TOT P50/SFR FIB P50) from the MPA-JHU catalogs. In the end, we obtain SFR measurements for 171 of the 516 post-starburst galaxies, including 79 post-starburst galaxies for which only SFR upper limit measurements are available. The bottom panel of Figure REF shows that the SFRs of our post-starburst galaxies decline over time. We discuss the timescale of this decline in Section REF .

input: Do nonlocal reductions actually preserve MNLS integrability, and can they be successfully applied across different models?
expected_output: The nonlocal reductions indeed preserve the integrability of the multicomponent nonlinear Schrödinger (MNLS) equations, and they can be successfully applied across different models. This is demonstrated by the analysis of special types of MNLS equations of KS type, which shows that they remain integrable even when nonlocal reductions are applied. The integrability of these models is maintained through the use of inverse scattering transform methods, allowing for the construction of soliton solutions and the analysis of their interactions. Furthermore, the application of nonlocal reductions to different models, such as the spinor Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) with various hyperfine states, has been shown to preserve their integrability, enabling the description of the dynamics and interaction of bright solitons with spin degrees of freedom.

input: What causes the variation in Fe ionization potential due to changes in plasma screening parameters, and how do these changes impact the overall ionization process?
expected_output: The variation in Fe ionization potential due to changes in plasma screening parameters is caused by the Debye-Hückel potential, which predicts a linear decrease of the ionization potential downshift with the plasma screening parameter. This decrease is more pronounced for larger ionic charges. The changes in plasma screening parameters impact the overall ionization process by reducing the ionization potentials and K-threshold energy positions, with the reductions increasing with the plasma screening parameter. For example, when going from an isolated ion to a plasma condition with a screening parameter of 0.1 a.u., the ionization potentials of Fe XXIV and Fe XXV are reduced by 64.5 and 67.8 eV, respectively. These shifts can affect atomic processes such as photoionization, radiative recombination, autoionization, and collisional excitation, and are not fully taken into account in current ionization balance calculations. The inclusion of electron-electron Debye screening, in addition to electron-nucleus screening, leads to a substantially less pronounced ionization potential lowering, ranging from 4% in Fe XXV to 50% in Fe XVII.
context:
Also, two big jumps are seen between {{formula:3e44d791-8c09-43f8-92ed-585db1aab75a}} and {{formula:542a1f47-9470-4dd0-a4e1-75b4a4d56514}} and between {{formula:64528e58-2255-4f23-bc73-65aaf836903a}} and {{formula:07e6784d-365d-4e75-8f25-9a9603cce88a}} . These correspond to respectively the transition from the closure of the K-shell and the starting of the filling of the L-shell, and the transition from the closure of the L-shell and the starting of the filling of the M-shell. These features are similar to the ones observed in the oxygen (Paper I) and iron isonuclear sequences (Papers II-IV).
[Figure: Ionization potential, E 0 E_0 in eV, in logarithmic scale as a function of the effective charge, Z eff Z_{\rm eff}, in ions belonging to the nickel isonuclear sequence. The NIST error bars are too small to appear in the figure.]In Figure REF , the MCDF/RATIP IP shift, {{formula:5dad5162-e687-44a8-96b0-7c5c98a8011e}} in eV, with respect to the isolated atom plasma condition ({{formula:cb083b47-bfb9-4799-b1e6-dc6929a18ee9}}  a.u.) is plotted as function of the effective charge in the same example (Nii–Nixxvii) for plasma screen parameters of 0.1 a.u. and 0.25 a.u. It can be seen that this quantity varies linearly with {{formula:4249b4cc-7cb2-4e1b-9f76-52fc493a1778}} with steeper slope for larger {{formula:ab36a94f-97b5-4b98-9719-2a3465f21182}} . Moreover,

The ionization potentials (IP) and K thresholds we have computed with screening parameters in the range {{formula:1f19e941-0f27-4365-be32-63b8689118a9}}  a.u. are summarized in Tables REF –REF . For the isolated ions ({{formula:5de271bd-fea7-4cf4-ac18-2e57c68b0772}} = 0) we reproduce the IPs listed in the NIST spectroscopic database to an accuracy better than 0.2%. The inclusion of the DH potential leads to reductions of the IP and K-threshold energy positions that increase with {{formula:2cf0bb48-0efa-402f-987e-a79f68212c52}} ; namely 3% and 8% for {{formula:125d65d0-bccf-482d-ae88-900b62bc0da3}} and {{formula:f8d6d4cb-b55d-4352-ac5e-e38246fdb53f}} , respectively, except for Fexxv for which the reduction is less than 2% due to its large IP {{formula:1b63a37e-a1f0-4fc6-9b78-a3e1849277e6}}  eV. For the same reason, the K-threshold reductions are only marginal ({{formula:ae112a03-f09f-4f32-8b05-1796f08403c6}} ).
[Table: Computed K-thresholds (eV) for Fexvii – Fexxv as a function of the plasma screening parameter μ\mu (a.u.).]This threshold lowering is a well-known phenomenon in dense-plasma physics, whose behavior is further illustrated in Figs. REF –REF . For each of the ionic species considered, the DH potential predicts a linear decrease of the IP downshift with {{formula:368c34b9-e9eb-48ae-b26e-d991f2d87bd4}} at a gradient that grows with ionic charge (see Fig. REF ); however, as shown in Fig. REF , the IP-shift variation with effective ionic charge {{formula:0104fe81-e272-4125-88d8-ece47bbd4144}} for a particular {{formula:39213c5e-e405-477b-bfc9-3b593a4d5d05}} is only moderate: {{formula:3626f932-3779-43df-b509-30989ec05a41}} . On the other hand, we find that, for any specific ionic species, the IP and K-threshold energy shifts are practically the same (see Fig. REF ).
[Figure: Ionization potential shifts in Fexvii – Fexxv as a function of the plasma screening parameter μ\mu .][Figure: IP (black points) and K-threshold (red points) energy shifts in Fe ions as a function of effective charge Z eff Z_{\rm eff} for μ=0.1\mu = 0.1 a.u. and μ=0.25\mu = 0.25  a.u.]In agreement with and as shown in Table REF , the inclusion of the electron–electron Debye screening, in addition to the electron–nucleus screening, leads to a substantially less pronounced IP lowering: 4% in Fexxv to 50% Fexvii.

The ionization potentials (IP) and K-thresholds obtained in the present work using different values of the plasma screening parameter are given in Table 2. First of all, it is worth mentioning that the ionization potentials obtained in our work for the isolated ions are in very good agreement (within 0.1 %) with the most accurate values published so far for Fe XXIV (IP = 2.045759(7) keV) [9] and Fe XXV (IP = 8.8281878(11) keV) [10]. Furthermore, when looking at Table 2, we note that, when going from {{formula:e3045e4a-b790-4629-bb44-e9a6ea723910}} = 0 (isolated ion) to {{formula:25737c2a-46a5-4148-a90d-7155c43ce18a}} = 0.1 (which corresponds to typical plasma conditions such as {{formula:24858c96-2297-459f-8cf3-bb292aaee620}} = 10{{formula:d49e2e88-cb8b-4f36-bc91-68762c3294cc}} K and {{formula:721e8b64-c44a-4046-8ed6-bb5f3294795d}} = 10{{formula:9f754425-5df2-4369-9116-38b0014a230e}} cm{{formula:da2714cd-04ac-4075-bf42-00564af6729a}} ), the ionization potentials of Fe XXIV and Fe XXV are reduced by 64.5 and 67.8 eV, while the corresponding K-thresholds are reduced by 65.1 and 67.8 eV, respectively. These shifts are illustrated in Figures 1 and 2. It is important to underline here that, if this effect of ionization potential depression in dense plasmas is a well-know process, this is not taken into account in a comprehensive way in current ionization balance calculations carried out in photoionized plasma modeling. As an example, in the code XSTAR [11,12], the treatment of continuum lowering for H- and He-isoelectronic sequences is based on fitting detailed cascade calculations incorporating about 10000 levels for each ion, with results applied to rates for fictitious superlevels. However, these results are only applicable up to densities of 10{{formula:21ccc67b-9c3a-43b9-a21b-458265018204}} cm{{formula:433a7779-d75b-40c0-92fe-8980115b19d9}} , which is not adequate for modeling iron lines from high density environments. In addition, the lowering of the ionization potentials can affect atomic processes such as photoionization/radiative recombination, autoionization/dielectronic recombination and collisional excitation/deexcitation.
[Table: Computed ionization potentials and the K-thresholds for Fe XXIV and Fe XXV ions as a function of the plasma screening parameter λ\lambda .]The wavelengths and radiative transition probabilities computed in our work for K{{formula:66224a6b-c957-45dc-9b62-1e3c13a115d0}} lines in Fe XXIV and Fe XXV are reported in Tables 3 and 4, repectively. These results were obtained using two different values of the plasma screening parameter, i.e. {{formula:4278f204-558e-47e3-9223-0f133dae9f78}} = 0 and 0.1 a.u.

input: How does the value of λ influence the variance of the estimator β̂, and what are the implications of this impact on the overall model performance?
expected_output: The value of λ, the overall smoothing parameter, influences the variance of the estimator β̂ through its effect on the weights w_i. As λ approaches 0, the weights w_i approach 0, and as λ approaches infinity, the weights w_i approach 1. This means that the variance of β̂ is affected by the smoothing parameter λ, with smaller values of λ resulting in a smaller variance. The implications of this impact on the overall model performance are that the choice of λ can affect the trade-off between bias and variance, with smaller values of λ potentially leading to a smaller variance but a larger bias, and larger values of λ potentially leading to a larger variance but a smaller bias. Therefore, the selection of an appropriate value for λ is crucial to achieve optimal model performance.

In contrast, Hyper-maxHML is a subset of formulas without least fixed-points, and its monitorability is derived through a synthesis function that produces monitors that return a verdict of "yes" or "no" based on the semantics of the formula. The key difference between the two approaches is that sHML^ω uses least fixed-points to describe liveness properties, whereas Hyper-maxHML does not, and instead focuses on regular properties of infinite traces that can be monitored for violations. Overall, while both fragments are monitorable, sHML^ω provides a more general framework for handling complex monitoring tasks, but at the cost of increased complexity in the synthesis function.

input: How can the enclosure method be applied to extract information on unknowns in heat and wave equations, and what are the key considerations for achieving accurate results across different equation types?
expected_output: The enclosure method can be applied to extract information on unknowns in heat and wave equations by utilizing an explicit method to approximate the value of the support function at a given direction of unknown discontinuity embedded in a heat conductive body from the temperature for a suitable heat flux on the lateral boundary for a fixed observation time. For heat equations, which are parabolic, the method involves considering a prototype of inverse initial boundary value problems whose governing equation is the heat equation. In the case of wave equations, the enclosure method is applied to inverse obstacle problems governed by the wave equation and the Maxwell system in the time domain. Key considerations for achieving accurate results across different equation types include the type of equation, whether it is elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic, and the specific formulation of the inverse problem, such as the initial and boundary conditions. Additionally, the choice of observation data and the fixed observation time are crucial for obtaining accurate results. By taking into account these factors, the enclosure method can be effectively applied to extract information on unknowns in various types of equations, including heat and wave equations.
context:
All of the applications of the enclosure method presented in the previous sections are devoted to
inverse problems governed by elliptic equations. This means that the observation data are independent
of time variable. However, there are a lot of important and interesting inverse problems whose governing
equations are not elliptic and involve time variable.
As a typical example, we can mention the inverse problem governed by the heat equation, the wave equation
or the Maxwell system.

The aim of this chapter is to make a review of the recent results using the
Enclosure Method on inverse obstacle problems governed by the wave equation and
the Maxwell system in time domain. We also describe some of unsolved problems
related to further possibility of the Enclosure Method itself.

This paper shows how the enclosure method which was originally introduced for
elliptic equations can be applied to inverse initial boundary value problems
for parabolic equations. For the purpose a prototype of inverse initial
boundary value problems whose governing equation is the heat equation is
considered. An explicit method to extract an approximation of the value of the
support function at a given direction of unknown discontinuity embedded in a
heat conductive body from the temperature for a suitable heat flux on the
lateral boundary for a fixed observation time is given.

input: What are the limitations of using cogenerating subcategories and exact functors in assessing cotorsion, and how do their interactions impact the overall effectiveness of this approach in practice?
expected_output: The limitations of using cogenerating subcategories and exact functors in assessing cotorsion lie in the requirement that the subcategory must be closed under countable products and the functors must be exact, which may not always be the case in practice. Additionally, the approach relies on the existence of enough injective objects in the category, which is not guaranteed. The interactions between cogenerating subcategories and exact functors can impact the effectiveness of this approach, as the closure of the subcategory under countable products and the exactness of the functors are crucial in ensuring that the quasi-isomorphism between complexes exists. Furthermore, the fact that the class of cotorsion contramodules is usually not generating in the category of contramodules can limit the applicability of this approach. However, as shown in Proposition 12.6, if the subcategory is cogenerating and closed under countable products, and the functors are exact, then for any complex in the category, there exists a quasi-isomorphism to a complex in the subcategory, which can be useful in practice. Overall, the effectiveness of this approach depends on the specific category and subcategory being considered, and careful analysis of the limitations and interactions is necessary to ensure its successful application.

Discussion
The proposed BiLMDM scheme relies on data
sharing among different frames by approximating each frame by an affine
combination of its neighboring frames on the manifold that describes locally
the MR data cloud. This manifold and sparse-approximation based recovery model
enables the reconstruction of desirable, good quality and artifact free MR
images from severely undersampled k-space measurements. The quality of the
reconstructed images and the corresponding performance in numbers discussed
under Sec.  is a testament to the fact that the BiLMDM
outperforms the competing state-of-the-art methods. BiLMDM has consistently
provided better results for both synthetically generated, retrospectively
undersampled as well as experimentally acquired, prospectively undersampled
cardiac cine data.
Methods like PS-Sparse and MLS have reconstructed desirable MR images in the
case of the MRXCAT phantom, under cartesian sampling trajectories; however,
they suffered severe motion blurring and deformations (enlargements) in the
case of the cardiac cine data retrospectively sampled via radial
trajectories. In contrast, SToRM produced good quality images for the data
using radial sampling but suffered severe spatial blurring and temporal
bleeding in the cases of Cartesian sampling. However, BiLMDM reconstructions
have been artifact free, without any temporal bleeding irrespective of what
sampling strategy was used to acquire data. Similar results to the ones
discussed here hold also for the sampling strategies not included in the
manuscript, for all employed algorithms. Even in the case of the
experimentally acquired data, where techniques like PS-Sparse, MLS, XD-GRASP
and LASSI suffered from some missing structures and distortions, while SToRM
suffered temporal blurring, BiLMDM produced images which seem to best preserve
the features of the cardiac structure spatially and temporally. BiLMDM seems
capable of reconstructing desirable MR images irrespective of the sampling
strategy into consideration, which appears to be a dominant factor in the
competing state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusions
This paper proposed the novel bi-linear modeling for data manifolds (BiLMDM); a
new framework for data reconstruction using manifold-learning and
sparse-approximation arguments.

input: Do linear and elliptic motions in Moving-MNIST-2 datasets actually improve model accuracy compared to static or other types of motion, and what are the implications of these motions on overall model performance?
expected_output: The Moving-MNIST-2 dataset is designed to test model performance on videos with varying motions, including linear and elliptic motions. The dataset consists of training, validation, and test sequences with variable numbers of MNIST digits moving within 50x50 frames. The use of linear and elliptic motions in the dataset is intended to simulate real-world video sequences, where object motion is typically smooth. The dataset's design allows for the evaluation of model performance based on metrics such as mean square error (MSE), peak signal-noise ratio (PSNR), and structure similarity (SSIM). The inclusion of linear and elliptic motions in the dataset can help improve model accuracy by providing a more realistic and challenging test environment. The elliptic motion, in particular, can help models learn to handle more complex and nuanced motion patterns. Overall, the use of linear and elliptic motions in the Moving-MNIST-2 dataset can have a positive impact on model performance, as it allows models to learn and generalize from a wider range of motion patterns, making them more robust and effective in real-world applications.
context:
The Moving-MNIST-2 dataset is generated by moving two digits of size
{{formula:2e3010e9-bb4d-4aae-8c00-041718582f5a}} in MNIST dataset within a {{formula:0e21ee54-85ce-49fc-9965-cb2165187b1a}} black canvas .
These digits are placed at a random initial location,
and move with constant velocity in the canvas and bounce when they reach the boundary.
In addition to the default velocity in the public generator ,
we increase the velocity to {{formula:50ed4c43-8ee1-4e8f-aced-beeac2f2816d}} and {{formula:20939aa6-21f7-43bb-b367-ae62c73cdec3}} to test all models on videos with stronger motions.
For each velocity, we generate 10,000 videos for training set, 3,000 for validation set, and 5,000 for test set,
where each video contains 20 frames.
All models are trained to the next 10 frames given 10 input frames, and we evaluate their performance
based on the metrics of mean square error (MSE), peak signal-noise ratio (PSNR)
and structure similarity (SSIM) .

Our datasets consist of {{formula:3baff004-2ee5-4b44-8626-1a46f85cc54a}} training, {{formula:b4839928-9577-4559-be03-9ab8245758a1}} validation, and {{formula:0edda7c6-0fb3-4df8-9c6f-29e1176e34d2}} test sequences with variable number of MNIST digits moving within 50x50 frames.
The length of the sequences is 20.
The number of digits in each sequence is sampled uniformly at random from {{formula:94a31b98-95f8-4473-a8bb-cfcd8e3c0971}} , but is fixed for each sequence.
MNIST digits for each sequence are sampled uniformly at random from the original MNIST dataset.
The MNIST digits in our test set are sampled only from the MNIST test set, whereas the ones in our training and validation sets are sampled only from the MNIST training set.Four versions of our dataset are determined by combination of two factors:whether digit motion is linear or elliptic

whether two digits in the first frame are allowed to overlapThe digits are placed at random position in the initial frame with the conditions of residing within the frame.
In non-overlapping first frame dataset two digits are not allowed to overlap in the first frame: i.e., they may not share non-zero intensity pixels (but may still overlap in further frames).In the dataset with linear motion, random velocity vector is sampled for each digit and kept constant during motion, except flipping the components of the velocity at the edges of the frame: when at least one pixel of the digit goes out of frame after a motion step, the digit bounces off the edge.In the dataset with elliptic motion, random elliptic trajectory is sampled for each digit such that a digit stays within the frame while moving along it.
Angular velocity of each individual object is also sampled randomly and kept constant throughout the sequence.As the velocity magnitudes are sampled from uniform distributions, while objects are moving, their positions take real values.
Instead of rounding the position to the nearest integer pixel and pasting the same constellation of pixels as in the original digit at a new discrete position, we maintain the real position values and through bilinear interpolation smoothen the digit motion.
We believe that this makes our datasets closer to real video sequences, where object motion is typically smooth.

This monochrome dataset consists in one or two training MNIST digits of size {{formula:b5a6e04f-8dc9-42f5-baf6-cd32f9d4c1a0}} moving linearly within a {{formula:82cafcdd-43a5-4e2b-b5c1-f596fb2684d7}} frame and randomly bouncing against its border, sampling a new direction and velocity at each bounce .
We use the same settings as , train all models on 15 timesteps, condition them at testing time on 5 frames, and predict either 20 (for the stochastic version) or 95 (for the deterministic version) frames.
Note that we adapted the dataset to sample more coherent bounces: the original dataset computes digit trajectories that are dependent on the chosen framerate, unlike our corrected version of the dataset.
We consequently retrained SVG on this dataset, obtaining comparable results as those originally presented by .
Test data were produced by generating a trajectory for each testing digit, and randomly pairwise combining these trajectories to produce 5000 testing sequences containing each two digits.We present in fig:mmnist-2d-s-sample-2,fig:mmnist-2d-s-sample-3,fig:mmnist-2d-s-sample-changing-digit,fig:mmnist-2d-s-sample-worst-result additional samples from SVG and our model on Stochastic Moving MNIST.In particular, fig:mmnist-2d-s-sample-changing-digit shows SVG changing a digit shape in the course of a prediction even though it does not cross another digit, whereas ours maintain the digit shape.
We assume that the advantage of our model comes from the latent nature of its dynamic and the use of a static content variable that is prevented from containing temporal information.
Indeed, even when the best sample from our model is not close from the ground truth of the dataset, like in fig:mmnist-2d-s-sample-worst-result, it still maintains the shapes of the digits.

input: What causes LLM's inherent instability to impact AutoBench's testbench generation accuracy, and how do different approaches to mitigating this instability affect the overall performance of AutoBench?
expected_output: The inherent instability of Large Language Models (LLMs) impacts AutoBench's testbench generation accuracy because it often leads to AutoBench failing in tasks that it is capable of solving, resulting in a low pass rate of the generated testbenches. This instability is caused by the LLMs' inability to consistently produce accurate results, which can be attributed to various factors such as the complexity of the input prompts, the quality of the training data, and the limitations of the LLMs' architecture. To mitigate this instability, AutoBench employs a self-enhancement process that includes syntax debugging, code completion, and scenario completion, which helps to refine the generated testbenches and improve their correctness. Additionally, the use of automatic code standardization and completion, as well as scenario checking, can also help to reduce the impact of LLM instability on AutoBench's performance. However, despite these efforts, AutoBench still lacks a mechanism to calibrate the generated testbenches, which is a significant challenge that needs to be addressed in future work. Exploring functional and coverage-aware self-correction and self-correction mechanisms may help to further enhance the accuracy of the generated testbenches and improve the overall performance of AutoBench.
context:
AutoBench is the first systematic and generic LLM-based testbench generation workflow.
This workflow consists primarily of three components: the Verilog driver track, the Python checker track, and the simple self-enhancement stages, as illustrated in Figure REF . The framework's sole input is the RTL specification in natural language. Initially, the driver track generates a list of test scenarios and subsequently produces the Verilog driver, which drives the DUT to generate output signals under these scenarios. A test scenario is characterized by a specific set of test stimuli, as shown in Fig. REF . Subsequently, the checker track produces a Python checker. The Python checker is a Python code that generates the reference signals of the testbench and checks the correctness of DUT's output signals. The integration of the driver and checker constitute the hybrid testbench, which is further refined through self-enhancement stages, including syntax debugging, code completion, and scenario completion.A significant challenge AutoBench faces is that it cannot check the correctness of the generated testbenches.
The inherent instability of LLMs often leads AutoBench to fail in tasks that it is capable of solving. Although AutoBench includes a syntax debugging stage to correct the syntax of generated testbenches, it still lacks a mechanism
to calibrate the generated testbenches, thus leading to a low pass rate.

In this section, the workflow of AutoBench is explained, including two parts: testbench forward generation in Section REF and testbench self-enhancement in Section REF , as is depicted in Fig. REF .
The information we have as input to the AutoBench workflow includes the DUT's problem description (or, in other words, RTL description) and the module header, as shown in Fig. REF , where the circuit type (combinational or sequential) is generated by the AutoBench workflow.
In generating a testbench, the DUT is not available to AutoBench. Otherwise, errors in the DUT may misguide the LLMs so that the resulting testbench may ignore errors.
The following explanation of AutoBench workflow is accompanied by an example of the testbench generation task gates100 originally from HDLBits .
The detailed demonstrations of this testbench generation task include prompts and LLM's responses in each stage, as shown in the Appendix.

With the generated driver and checker, a self-enhancement process is undertaken to improve the testbench's correctness, as depicted in the right part of Fig. REF . Automatic code standardization and completion are performed according to predetermined formatting rules. For the checker, scenario checking is conducted to ensure that all scenarios in the list are present in the final driver code. Subsequently, both codes are executed to detect any syntax errors. The LLM attempts to resolve these errors using debugging information. If it fails after several attempts, the system reboots at the code generation process from Stage 4 or Stage 5, depending on the code type.The final revised and corrected codes will constitute the hybrid testbench produced by AutoBench. The implementation of AutoBench is accessible as open-source on https://github.com/AutoBench/AutoBench. Future work will involve exploring functional and coverage-aware self-correction and self-correction mechanisms to further enhance the accuracy of the generated testbenches.

expected_output: The Palais-Smale (PS) condition plays a crucial role in ensuring sequence convergence by providing a framework for establishing the existence of convergent subsequences in various mathematical contexts. In the context of functional analysis and optimization, the PS condition ensures that a sequence of approximate critical points of a functional converges to a genuine critical point. This is achieved by requiring that any sequence satisfying certain conditions, such as boundedness and gradient convergence, has a convergent subsequence. The key properties that make the PS condition effective include its ability to establish compactness, weak convergence, and strong convergence of sequences, which are essential in a wide range of mathematical frameworks, including calculus of variations, partial differential equations, and optimization theory. By leveraging these properties, the PS condition enables researchers to establish the existence of solutions to various problems, including those involving nonlinear equations and variational inequalities. Furthermore, the PS condition has been adapted and generalized to accommodate different mathematical settings, such as constrained optimization, non-smooth analysis, and infinite-dimensional spaces, making it a fundamental tool in modern mathematics.

input: How does dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies compare to static anisotropy in terms of wave propagation characteristics?
expected_output: Dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies in the context of elastic wave scattering exhibits distinct wave propagation characteristics compared to static anisotropy. In the vicinity of the cut-off frequencies, specifically at ω = √6 for pressure waves and ω = 3√2/2 for shear waves, the dispersion surfaces of the bulk lattice display non-circular slowness contours. These contours lead to preferential directions of wave propagation, resulting in dynamic anisotropy. This phenomenon is manifested in the scattered field through effects such as star-shaped scattered waveforms, negative reflection, and negative refraction. In contrast, static anisotropy refers to the directional dependence of material properties, which can also influence wave propagation. However, dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies is a unique feature that arises from the topology of the dispersion surfaces and is not directly related to static material anisotropy. The dynamic anisotropy observed in this context is a consequence of the frequency-dependent behavior of the lattice, whereas static anisotropy is a property of the material itself, independent of frequency.

Further, there is a cut-off frequency at \omega =3\sqrt{2}/2 for the lower dispersion surface, which is associated with shear waves at low-frequencies. Below this frequency, one can penetrate the inertial defect with a combination two different waveforms, whereas this is only possible with one waveform in the range 3\sqrt{2}/2<\omega <\sqrt{6}.Close to the specified cut-off frequencies within the bulk pass-band, we may observe dynamic anisotropy in the scattering response of the inertial defect. This is connected with the topology of the dispersion surfaces for the bulk lattice (see (REF )). Those surfaces exhibit non-circular slowness contours near the cut-off frequencies. These contours promote preferential directions of wave propagation in the lattice that appear in the scattered field. expected_output: Antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects can be understood across different filling ranges by analyzing the behavior of the magnon dispersion relations and the spin stiffness. The renormalization effects become more pronounced at long wavelengths, particularly at the Brillouin zone center, where the spin stiffness decreases with doping and increases with the interaction strength. To analyze these variations, methods such as inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements and perturbative expansions can be employed. INS measurements can provide direct information about the magnon dispersion relations, while perturbative expansions can be used to calculate the renormalization effects and the spin stiffness. Additionally, comparisons with experimental results from single crystals of antiferromagnetic heavy fermions, such as CeIn3, can help to validate the theoretical models and provide insight into the behavior of the magnon renormalization effects. By combining these methods, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects and their variations across different filling ranges.

input: What are the advantages and limitations of using Lagrange multipliers to enhance stability in Stokes equations, and how do different implementations perform in practice across various fluid dynamics applications?
expected_output:
The use of Lagrange multipliers to enhance stability in Stokes equations offers several advantages, including the ability to enforce boundary conditions and improve pressure-robustness, which is essential for accurately simulating fluid dynamics. One of the primary benefits of this approach is that it allows for the creation of a weakly coupled velocity error estimate, where the velocity error's dependence on viscosity is compensated by a higher-order power of the discretization parameter. Additionally, the introduction of Lagrange multipliers can lead to a more stable and optimally convergent method, as demonstrated in the analysis of LBB-unstable and LBB-stable velocity-pressure FE pairs.

However, the implementation of Lagrange multipliers also has some limitations. For instance, the method can be sensitive to the choice of the Lagrange multiplier space and the stabilization technique used. Moreover, the addition of Lagrange multipliers can increase the complexity of the resulting matrices, which can impact the computational efficiency of the method. Different implementations of Lagrange multipliers, such as the Haslinger-Renard method and the Burman-Hansbo method, have been proposed and analyzed, each with its strengths and weaknesses.

In practice, the performance of Lagrange multipliers in enhancing stability in Stokes equations can vary depending on the specific application and the characteristics of the problem. For example, in fluid-structure interaction problems, the use of Lagrange multipliers can be particularly beneficial in handling the complex boundary conditions and the movement of the solid. On the other hand, in problems with complex geometries or high Reynolds numbers, the method may require additional stabilization techniques or modifications to ensure optimal performance.

Overall, the use of Lagrange multipliers to enhance stability in Stokes equations is a powerful tool that can be effective in a wide range of fluid dynamics applications. However, its implementation requires careful consideration of the specific problem characteristics and the choice of the Lagrange multiplier space and stabilization technique. Further research and development are needed to fully explore the potential of this approach and to address the remaining challenges and limitations.

into a finite number of strictly star shaped domains; the number
of star shaped domains is generally unbounded as {{formula:5924bcbc-da82-4677-8a7c-922d33259491}} .
This issue can be circumvented with pressure-stabilization, but at the price
of additional consistency errors and poor conservation properties.
We address this stability issue by designing the computational mesh
such that it inherits a macro element structure and
applying the framework developed in 
for Stokes pairs on unfitted domains. Doing so, we show
that the resulting pair is uniformly stable on the unfitted domain with respect
to the discretization parameter.The second difficulty of a boundary correction
method for the Stokes problem is its lack of pressure-robustness.
This feature is not due to the boundary correction per se, but rather
due to the weak enforcement of boundary conditions via penalization.
In particular, a divergence-free method for the Stokes problem
with weak enforcement of the boundary conditions is not pressure robust.
We mitigate the lack of pressure robustness in the scheme by introducing
an additional Lagrange multiplier that enforces the boundary conditions of the normal component of the velocity.
The Lagrange multiplier space consists of continuous piecewise quadratic polynomials
with respect to the boundary partition, and the Lagrange multiplier is an approximation to the pressure (modulo
an additive constant) restricted to the computational boundary.
The Lagrange multiplier ameliorates the lack of pressure robustness of the method
and leads to a weakly coupled velocity error estimate; the velocity error's dependence on the viscosity
is compensated by a higher-order power of the discretization parameter {{formula:c25b57e2-9842-4172-891b-b0e8c40edfb7}} .
We remark that Lagrange multipliers within boundary correction schemes have been proposed and studied in , 
for the Poisson problem.The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
In the next section, we state the Stokes problem,
the computational mesh, and the boundary transfer operator.
In Section , we state the finite element method
and show that the scheme yields exactly divergence–free velocity approximations.
Section proves several inf-sup conditions and
the well-posedness of the method.
In Section , we prove optimal order convergence provided
the exact solution is sufficiently smooth. Finally, in Section 
we perform some numerical experiments which verify the theoretical results,
and give some concluding remarks in Section .

Several stabilization techniques were therefore proposed in the literature, using either Lagrange multipliers , or a Nitsche-like method to take into account the boundary conditions on {{formula:d1a21d79-4eb5-4af1-959e-1d92e67b4c5a}} . We shall be concerned in this chapter only with the methods based on Lagrange multipliers. Firstly, we adapt the method of Haslinger-Renard (cf. for the Poisson problem) to Stokes equations. The method is based on a Barbosa-Hughes stabilization on {{formula:d9071f8a-f27b-4061-ac1c-d804cd5ab2a7}} with additional local treatment on badly cut mesh elements. An extension to Stokes equations was already presented in but the analysis there relied on a number of hypotheses, difficult to verify. In this paper, we present a complete theoretical analysis in two cases :LBB-unstable velocity-pressure FE pairs, namely, {{formula:77636d33-508f-4199-8131-6e315b4d9388}} or {{formula:6226b96f-6011-4b2f-9bcc-ee3a3e99affe}} elements. A stabilization is needed in this case even on a fitted mesh. We shall show, that adding the well known stabilization terms such as Brezzi-Pitkäranta for {{formula:8525a7ae-a2b9-45a0-ac18-dbbb0312424d}} elements (or interior penalty for {{formula:e4a0d1ca-e371-4b40-a3f9-583666c59e07}} elements) to a Haslinger-Renard fictitious domain method, as in , makes it stable and optimally convergent.

LBB-stable velocity-pressure FE pairs, namely, {{formula:6091f470-1858-41e3-b989-0cfc00120814}} Taylor-Hood elements. We show that a version of the method above (with and additional pressure stabilization on {{formula:8d384dff-3906-4162-902c-d93e27cb406e}} but avoiding stabilization over the whole domain {{formula:171f5b00-0dee-4f69-99f0-6bfed0c41d21}} ) is also stable and optimally convergent. Our proofs are presented here only in the 2D case and under some additional assumptions on the mesh.We generalize moreover a method by Burman-Hansbo to Stokes equations. This is also a fictitious domain method with Lagrange multipliers. Unlike the method by Haslinger-Renard (where the stabilization comes by enforcing (REF ) on {{formula:be175138-5a7b-450c-8ea3-64f497d74add}} and thus involves all the variables {{formula:b83d3687-a3de-485b-a829-ec152732b832}} , {{formula:0af8d9a7-0b97-49d3-9feb-fc628109350d}} , {{formula:af8f22c6-2144-40ab-b7a2-d3e47a592594}} ), one stabilizes here only the multiplier {{formula:0ee6d364-bba4-4ad9-91f3-03b7bb2b2784}} by enforcing its continuity in some sense, so that the structure of resulting matrices is simpler. Fortunately, much of the theory outlined above can be reused for the analysis of this method.

For Stokes problem which is the corner stone of computations in fluid dynamics, we have proposed a fictitious domain method based on extended finite element method. Dirichlet boundary conditions at the interface is made using Lagrange multiplier. Additional stabilization term is used to ensure an inf-sup condition and to obtain an optimal convergence of the normal trace of the Cauchy stress tensor {{formula:0f744f9e-6e89-46b2-9af5-7500e97e2fff}} . The mathematical analysis is presented. We have carried out numerical simulations to compare the new method with the classical finite element approximation based on uncut mesh and with the same approach without the introduction of the stabilization term. Computations of convergence rates have been performed and have especially underlined the interest of the stabilization technique in order to compute a good approximation of the normal trace of the Cauchy stress tensor. Besides, this stabilization technique allows a robust behavior of this quantity when the position of the solid changes.In a near future, we plan to perform simulations in an unsteady framework, by solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a domain where the solid is moving and deforming itself. Our method is particularly interesting in fluid-structure problems for which the role of the boundary is central, like for instance when the shape of the boundary is the unknown of a control problem.
